readme.text:
# Plectis Atlas Read the papers in [OpenAI’s mathematics release](https://github.com/openai/math), compare their theorems with statements written in Lean, and read independent assessments. Lean is software for writing mathematical statements and verifying proofs. Plectis Atlas brings these sources together in an independent website, naming who compared the statements or ran a proof-verification program and what their reports establish. **[Explore the map ↗](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/)**   [Read a paper](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/papers/Quasipolynomial-Bounds-for-Arithmetic-Progressions-September-23-2026.html)   [Browse by subject](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/explain.html)   [Contribute](CONTRIBUTING.md)   [Build it locally](#build-it-yourself) *OpenAI’s release, grouped by discipline. Each dot is a “family”, OpenAI’s group of related papers. Colours show whether MathVet and cert-machine agree that the Lean statements express the advertised result. Outlines mark families with no Lean statement.* The mathematics is OpenAI’s and the cited authors’ work. Independent assessments and reports of proof verification come from [MathVet](https://math.vet), [Carlos Toledo’s cert-machine](https://github.com/carlostoledo1891/cert-machine) and [Neal McBurnett’s Lean tooling](https://github.com/nealmcb/openai-math-lean-tooling). Atlas links their reports and has not repeated their work. [Sources and credits](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/sources.html). ## Why it exists OpenAI’s release contains PDFs, their TeX typesetting source, a catalogue and Lean files. The relevant information is spread across them: the paper’s theorem, a possible Lean counterpart, OpenAI’s note on what the Lean statement expresses, and independent assessments or proof-verification reports. Atlas brings those sources onto each family’s page and links the papers that cite one another. Families without Lean remain visible. You can read the website without installing anything. *Inside a family: the paper’s theorems beside possible Lean counterparts. A dashed line is a match selected from shared wording, with no recorded review of whether the statements mean the same thing.* ## What you can do | Start here | What you get | |---|---| | [The map](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/) | Browse disciplines and families, search for a theorem or paper, and follow citations. Each family shows its papers and possible matches between paper theorems and Lean statements. | | [The reciprocal-sum family](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/families/159.html) | The paper’s claim beside its linked Lean statement, OpenAI’s note on what that statement expresses, independent assessments and original proof-verification reports. | | [A paper](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/papers/Quasipolynomial-Bounds-for-Arithmetic-Progressions-September-23-2026.html) | A full reading page typeset from the paper’s TeX, with linked theorems, equations, cross-references and citations. Any conversion gap is listed on the page; the PDF stays the reference. | | [A Lean statement](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/statements/ErdosReciprocal.html) | The complete statement file, links to definitions that Atlas can identify, proof-verification reports and possible paper matches. | | [Sources and independent assessments](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/sources.html) | Who compared the statements, verified proofs or calculated finite claims, with links to the original reports. | *OpenAI’s paper, displayed in Atlas, with its original PDF and TeX source beside it. Follow its family link to the Lean statements and attributed outside readings. The PDF remains the reference.* Three independent groups report running [Comparator](https://github.com/leanprover/comparator) on the recorded release version: runs for 409 of the 416 statement files were accepted by at least one group, and 179 by all three. Comparator verifies the proof of a configured theorem; for files that configure only definitions, it compares their names and types. Acceptance does not establish that a statement means the same thing as the paper’s theorem. Two of them, [MathVet](https://math.vet) and Carlos Toledo’s [cert-machine](https://github.com/carlostoledo1891/cert-machine), also assessed whether every family’s Lean statements express the result OpenAI advertises, independently of each other. They agree on 220 of the 242 families both read and disagree on 22; each family page shows both readings. ## The release in numbers | In the pinned release | Explore | |---|---| | **372 result families** across 17 disciplines | [Browse by subject](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/explain.html) | | **719 current manuscripts** | [Read the papers through their families](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/explain.html) | | **416 Lean statement files** | [Inspect the formal statements](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/statements.html) | | **16,077 resolved references** to work outside the collection | [Follow the citations](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/references-outside.html) | All counts describe the release at the commit in [`upstream.json`](upstream.json). The site’s [Numbers page](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/numbers.html) gives each number’s definition and the records behind it.
Full counts, coverage and reading-page checks - **372 result families** in 17 disciplines, from **719 current manuscripts** (3 more were withdrawn and 27 earlier editions remain in the collection). - **416 Lean statement files for Comparator**, 189 of them named in OpenAI's list of main results (200 entries). 242 families have an OpenAI note linking at least one statement file and explaining what it expresses, and those notes name 339 current manuscripts as accompanying papers. - **10 statement files** use only Mathlib, Lean's mathematical library, and add no local definitions or notation. The median file adds 13 local declarations (definitions, structures, instances, notation and similar), and the largest (EditApproximation) adds 1,212. These determine what the formal statement means, so a comparison with the paper must include them. - **386 manuscripts** cite other manuscripts in the collection (586 citation links in the current extraction; the Atlas baseline inventory counts 579). 217 of them cite at least one manuscript without associated Lean. - **16,077 resolved references** to work outside the collection, which group automatically into 11,019 works (by DOI, then arXiv identifier, then title; the grouping is unaudited). - The TeX sources of the current manuscripts contain 2,255 theorem, 4,745 proposition, 1,267 corollary and 12,397 lemma environments, repeated statements included. - **AI-drafted comparisons.** Of 416 statement files, an AI agent classified 307 as stating a paper's theorem, 21 part of one, 28 a consequence, 24 a weaker form and 35 a supporting result; for 1 OpenAI's note leaves it unclear. The agent classified each file from OpenAI's note, quoting the note. No human review of these classifications is recorded. - **Independent assessments.** [MathVet](https://math.vet) and Carlos Toledo's [cert-machine](https://github.com/carlostoledo1891/cert-machine) each assessed whether every family's Lean statements express the result OpenAI advertises, independently of OpenAI and of each other. Their findings, in their own terms, are on each family page and in the Families list. - **Every paper in the browser.** 696 of the 719 current manuscripts have a full reading page made from their TeX, with formulas that KaTeX can typeset and links that resolve to their references, citations and theorems (figures are shown as placeholders); the other 23 have a reading page with a banner listing what did not convert. These tests validate the conversion, not the mathematics. They use the same KaTeX version as the site. The PDF stays the reference (`data/paper_acceptance.json`). Counted by Statement Map from [openai/math at `fd4aeeb2ee4f`](https://github.com/openai/math/tree/fd4aeeb2ee4fc729c18d98444fed42fd0529eeeb), generation `e44fe048bf34`. The unit, rule, state and credit behind each number, and its members, are on the site's Numbers page.
## One result, side by side The [reciprocal-sum family](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/families/159.html) shows how the pieces fit: Erdős’s conjecture that a set of positive integers whose reciprocals diverge contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, the paper whose corollary states it, and the Lean statement OpenAI’s proof is checked against.
Read the paper’s statement, the Lean challenge and OpenAI’s scope note **Family 159: Erdős’s reciprocal-sum conjecture and quasipolynomial Szemerédi bounds.** The paper, [*Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions*](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/fd4aeeb2ee4fc729c18d98444fed42fd0529eeeb/preprints/Quasipolynomial-Bounds-for-Arithmetic-Progressions-September-23-2026/paper.pdf), states: > **Theorem** (label `ap:main`). For each fixed integer $k\ge3$ there are constants > $C_k,c_k,\varepsilon_k>0$ such that, for every $N\ge2$, > $$ > r_k(N)\le C_kN\exp(-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k}). > $$ > Equivalently, there is $A_k\ge1$ such that an $\alpha$-dense subset > of $[N]$ contains a nonconstant $k$-term progression whenever > $$ > \log N\ge A_k(2+\log(1/\alpha))^{A_k}, > \qquad 0<\alpha\le1. > $$ > > **Corollary** (label `ap:reciprocal`). Every set $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ with $\sum_{a\in A}a^{-1}=\infty$ contains nonconstant arithmetic progressions of every finite length. The Lean statement [`ErdosReciprocal`](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/fd4aeeb2ee4fc729c18d98444fed42fd0529eeeb/lean/ComparatorChallenges/ErdosReciprocal.lean), the fixed statement Comparator checks OpenAI's proof against when it is run (3 local vocabulary declarations; allowed axioms `propext`, `Quot.sound`, `Classical.choice`; no definition holes): ```lean def HasAP (A : Set ℕ) (k : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ a d : ℕ, 0 < d ∧ ∀ i < k, a + i * d ∈ A noncomputable def reciprocalTerm (A : Set ℕ) (n : ℕ) : ℝ := by classical exact if n ∈ A then (n : ℝ)⁻¹ else 0 def ReciprocalProgressionTheorem : Prop := ∀ A : Set ℕ, ¬ Summable (reciprocalTerm A) → ∀ k : ℕ, HasAP A k theorem manuscriptReciprocalProgressionTheorem : ReciprocalProgressionTheorem := by sorry ``` This challenge file leaves the proof as `sorry` by design. OpenAI's proof lives in the solution module `OAI.Combinatorics.Progressions.Main`, and if Comparator accepts a run, the proof establishes exactly the statement above using only the allowed axioms. MathVet and Neal McBurnett report re-running Comparator on it and accepting the proof. OpenAI's scope note for this family: > Erdős's reciprocal-sum conjecture asks whether every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length. The formalization proves this statement: for every requested length, such a set contains a progression with positive common difference. The selected theorem is the reciprocal-sum consequence. The paper's quantitative upper bound for the largest progression-free subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is outside this statement.
A successful proof check establishes the formal statement it checked. Whether that statement matches the paper is a separate judgement. Re-runs and readings are credited to the people who report them. Pairings the atlas proposed automatically, and scope readings an AI agent drafted, are labelled as such until a person reviews them. For a paper’s reading page, the PDF stays the reference. ## Read the website as an agent The [website and map are agent-navigable](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/agents.md). Start with [llms.txt](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/llms.txt), then fetch the map's [overview](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/data/universe-data.json) and [parts](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/data/universe-parts.json) JSON. They expose every map node and its relationships, with stable source IDs, page links and a shared generation. The guide explains the index joins and includes a runnable Python traversal. ```sh curl --fail --location https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/llms.txt curl --fail --location https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/agents.md ``` No browser or JavaScript is needed. These static text routes reuse the map's existing exports and add no data request to a human page load. Preserve the source pin and evidence labels: citations are not proof dependencies, and candidate paper-to-Lean pairings remain unreviewed. ## Contribute Pick a passage you are reading and say what is wrong, unclear or missing, with its location and what you checked. You can [open a note](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-atlas/issues/new?template=report-a-problem.yml) from the browser. Accepted contributions are credited beside the work they improve. Agents can file [unreviewed source, rendering, navigation or reproduction observations](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-atlas/issues/new?template=agent-observation.yml) from a disclosed public account when their operator and platform permit it. Include the exact source and page, revision, checks and uncertainty; this issue route does not claim human review. For more, [explain a result](skills/explain-a-result/SKILL.md), [compare a statement with its paper](skills/check-a-statement/SKILL.md), [trace an earlier source](skills/trace-a-credit/SKILL.md) or [replay a proof check](skills/replay-a-proof/SKILL.md). The [contributor guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) covers formats, credit and review. **Working with an agent?** Open this repository in Codex, Claude Code or Cursor and ask it to start with [`start-here`](skills/start-here/SKILL.md); the [agent instructions](AGENTS.md) route each task to its skill. A named person stands behind each signed contribution and says how AI was used. ## Repository | Folder | What lives here | |---|---| | [contributions/](contributions/) | Explanations, statement checks, credits and replay receipts | | [curated/](curated/) | Attributed outside reports and draft scope readings | | [backend/](backend/) | Pinned evidence records exported by Statement Map | | [data/](data/) | Generated source indexes and paper-rendering metadata | | [site/](site/README.md) | Page copy, styles and browser code | | [scripts/](scripts/README.md) | Builders, importers and checks; regression suites in `scripts/tests/` | | [docs/images/](docs/images/) | Light and dark README screenshots | | [docs/](docs/README.md) | Documentation index and architecture guide | | [skills/](skills/) | Task instructions for coding agents | | [.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/](.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/) | Issue forms for reader notes and unreviewed agent observations | The [documentation index](docs/README.md) collects the guides for contributors and developers. `python3 scripts/check_repository_structure.py` enforces these roles in CI; it checks Git candidates, including staged additions, while ignoring generated website output. ## How it is built The site is static: Python builds it from a pinned commit of OpenAI’s release and a checked-in export from **Statement Map**, the separate backend that joins papers, Lean statements, citations and outside reports. Its [export is included here](backend/EXPORT.json), so you can rebuild the site without running the backend. The site builders check data integrity and page rendering; they do not run Lean or Comparator. Papers are typeset in the browser with KaTeX. The build checks formula conversion with the same KaTeX version the site loads; conversion acceptance is separate from checking the mathematics. Reading the published site needs no installation or account. For a complete local copy, install **Python 3.10 or newer, Git and Node.js**. The core scripts use Python’s standard library, and KaTeX is included; there is no `pip install` or `npm install` step. The source-fetch step needs a network connection and creates a sibling `openai-math-upstream` checkout. ```sh git clone https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-atlas cd plectis-atlas python3 scripts/reader.py sh scripts/fetch_upstream.sh python3 scripts/build_site.py python3 scripts/build_papers.py --jobs 2 python3 scripts/build_universe.py python3 scripts/check_paper_links.py site/_build python3 -m http.server -d site/_build ``` Open [localhost:8000](http://localhost:8000). Keep that build order: `build_site.py` clears its output before the paper reader adds its pages. To work on copy or layout without downloading paper sources, use the [quick preview](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md#quick-preview-without-paper-sources). The [architecture guide](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) explains the data boundaries, metadata refresh and checks. ## For producers of formal mathematics If you release Lean alongside papers, [the alignment proposal](ALIGNMENT.md) describes optional `formalization.yaml` fields for linking each printed claim to its Lean declaration. It also describes how readers can return checked work to you. ## Credits and related work The atlas reads [OpenAI’s release](https://github.com/openai/math) and brings in the work of [MathVet](https://math.vet), Carlos Toledo’s [cert-machine](https://github.com/carlostoledo1891/cert-machine) and Neal McBurnett’s [Lean tooling](https://github.com/nealmcb/openai-math-lean-tooling). Each finding is credited where it is shown, with a link to the source’s own record; the [Sources page](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/sources.html) lists them all and [NOTICE](NOTICE) records imported material and licences.
Related projects and the writing behind the design | Project | Its work and the atlas’s use of it | | --- | --- | | [OpenAI mathematics release](https://github.com/openai/math) | The papers, catalogue, scope notes, formal statements and release history the atlas reads. Every page links back to the pinned source. | | [MathVet](https://github.com/mathvet/mathvet), Carlos Toledo’s [cert-machine](https://github.com/carlostoledo1891/cert-machine) and Neal McBurnett’s [Lean tooling](https://github.com/nealmcb/openai-math-lean-tooling) | Outside statement readings and reported re-runs, shown in their own terms with their scope and disagreements. | | [Comparator](https://github.com/leanprover/comparator) | The tool that checks a solution against its challenge statement in the reported re-runs. Building this website does not run it. | | [formalization.yaml](https://github.com/mathlib-initiative/formalization.yaml) | The metadata standard the alignment proposal builds on. | | Patrick Massot’s [leanblueprint](https://github.com/PatrickMassot/leanblueprint) | Authoring infrastructure that links a project’s informal blueprint to its Lean as the project is written. | | [Cited by AGI](https://citedbyagi.com/) | Traces the bibliographic citations in the release. | Henry Cohn’s [essay on the technical debt of AI-generated mathematics](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/09/15/the-technical-debt-of-ai-generated-mathematics/) argues for explanations a reader can reconstruct and use. Thomas Hales’s [account of Lean’s reliability](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/10/09/what-mathematicians-should-know-about-the-lean-theorem-proverquestions-of-reliability-and-ai/) separates checking a proof from deciding what a formal statement means. [Responsible Release of AI-Generated Mathematics](https://agmai.org/general-sep29/) asks for attribution, clear exposition and support for human understanding. They inform the emphasis on readable explanations, attribution and careful interpretation of formal statements. None is an endorsement or review of this atlas. The [About page](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/about.html) says more.
## Videos and related projects | Film | What it covers | Publication | | --- | --- | --- | | [Introduction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uO2lbstEH9M) | Will’s overview of tools for inspecting work produced with AI agents, including CodeMap, the mathematics papers, Atlas, Demo Take and Safety Core. | Available | | [Atlas walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uLHWmBLsAHE) | Search for the result about π and the Flint Hills series, compare MathVet’s and Carlos Toledo’s reasons for different coverage labels, follow the original reports, and see how to offer a correction or explanation. | Available | ### Where Atlas fits Plectis is Will Cook’s programme of research and software built with AI agents. The aim is to make the resulting work understandable enough for other people to inspect, question and build on. Atlas applies that approach to other authors’ mathematics, keeping the original papers and outside assessments attributed. | Related project | Why follow it | | --- | --- | | [Plectis Erdős](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos) · [research website](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/maths/) | The original eight-problem research corpus whose paper-to-Lean records informed Atlas. | | [Plectis Erdős Lean](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos-lean) | Lean proofs and Comparator checks for selected results from that corpus. | Explore the [research corpus](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos) and the [Plectis website](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/). ## Licences and independence Report vulnerabilities through the [private security route](SECURITY.md). Plectis Atlas is independent of OpenAI and is not affiliated with or endorsed by it. Quoted release material is copyright OpenAI, reproduced under Apache-2.0 from the pinned source. Original Atlas code and documentation are Apache-2.0; contributed explanations are CC BY 4.0. Imported material retains its own terms, including MIT and SIL Open Font License components. See [the licence](LICENSE), [attribution notice](NOTICE) and [source and citation guide](docs/ATTRIBUTION.md). ## Author Made by [Will Cook](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/). The atlas grew out of the paper-to-Lean records built for [Plectis’s research on eight Erdős problems](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/maths/). The results it shows belong to their authors. To cite the atlas, use [`CITATION.cff`](CITATION.cff). Cite the original paper or outside report as well when relying on its result; the Atlas citation does not replace those credits.

repositories.summary: See where your AI assistant’s safety rules apply and what checks them.

readme.text: # Safety Core **An editable rulebook and practical checks for your own coding-agent setup.** [Plectis website](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/) · [Get started](#what-happens-after-cloning) · [Documentation](docs/README.md) · [Agent skill](skills/safety-core/SKILL.md) · [Architecture](docs/maintainers/design.md) · [Videos](#videos-and-related-projects) The website is agent-readable through its [navigation guide](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/llms.txt). For this repository's map, the [graph schema](docs/reference/graph-schema.md) and [sample JSON](examples/graph.sample.json) expose the configured relationships without a browser. Improved with public feedback from **Skitter** (secret-read approval and home/root reasons), **glue72desk** (a prohibitions pass can omit a requested issue) and **adctx** (constructed malformed-type cases beyond a collected corpus). [Contribution details and source reports](CONTRIBUTING.md#feedback-contributions). *Synthetic demo, captured 15 October 2026. The full overview shows seven axioms, fifteen principles and their routes to repository files. It shows configured guidance and checks; execution is not assessed.* Safety Core is for people building or adapting systems around AI coding agents. You choose the principles, connect them to places in your repository, and inspect which ones are instructions, reminders or executable checks. The starting rules cover ordinary concerns: keep people in control, do useful work without constant permission prompts, preserve tests, keep secrets out, and report results honestly. It adapts selected ideas from [Anthropic's Claude Constitution](https://www.anthropic.com/constitution) to repository work. You can revise that starting point for your project. It does not train a model or implement the complete Constitution. Claude Code runs the runtime hooks. Codex and other agents can read the generated instructions; that does not make them run those hooks. ## What happens after cloning? Safety Core is a toolkit you copy into a project. It does not run an agent itself. ```sh git clone https://github.com/wcook04/safety-core.git mkdir my-project cd my-project git init python3 ../safety-core/safety.py init --target . python3 .doctrine/safety.py check ``` You need Python 3.11 or later and Git. Safety Core needs no Python packages or API key. Your chosen agent has its own installation and account requirements. Setup copies the tools and rules into `.doctrine/`, generates agent instructions, and configures Claude Code hooks. It preserves existing settings and text outside managed regions. Review the setup files, then open your agent in `my-project/` and give it an ordinary task. For an existing project, run `init --target .` from its directory. Once initialized, the project has its own copy; it does not depend on the original clone. | Part | What happens | |---|---| | `.doctrine/doctrine.toml` | You edit the local principles, paths, sources and supported hook modes. | | `AGENTS.md` | The builder writes a short entry card and a table of where rules apply. Supported agents read it as instructions. | | `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/` | Claude Code receives the entry card and path-specific guidance. | | `.claude/settings.json` | Configures Claude Code to call the local Python hooks at tool and session events. | | `.doctrine/sessions/` | Hooks record selected command results and edits locally, ignored by Git. | | `check`, `explain` and `map` | Inspect generated instructions, rule connections and recognized configuration. | The full Constitution is reference material. Agents receive your generated local rulebook; Safety Core does not paste the whole Constitution into every prompt. ## Customize, build, inspect Edit **`.doctrine/doctrine.toml`**, then run: ```sh python3 .doctrine/safety.py build python3 .doctrine/safety.py check python3 .doctrine/safety.py explain src/app.py python3 .doctrine/safety.py map --serve --open ``` The map connects axioms (why), principles (what), routes (where), sources and mechanisms (how). Inspect a file to see its rules and their configured support. Setup keeps routes that match the project at that time. Add routes as you add tests, migrations or infrastructure. Edit the rulebook and rebuild; do not hand-edit generated instruction regions or `.claude/rules/doctrine-*.md`. You can change existing hook modes, such as asking versus blocking. A new sentence does not create a new blocker: a new hard rule needs an executable mechanism and tests. The [adoption walkthrough](docs/guides/adoption.md) demonstrates a mode change and its observable effect without performing a real publication. ## A normal task and a consequential action For a bug fix, the agent can read code, make a reversible change and run tests without Safety Core asking at every step. Editing a routed test file delivers a reminder; recognized shell results become records for checking final claims. For a release, the agent can prepare, test and inspect a dry run. A recognized `npm publish` triggers the default approval prompt. The hook recognizes the command, not whether an earlier conversation already authorized it. You can inspect these responses without a model or a real release: ```sh # Run from the Safety Core clone. bash examples/demo.sh ``` The demo uses synthetic events and temporary repositories, with no external publication. It tests hook responses, not delivery through your agent host. ## What the checks actually cover Runtime hooks target **Claude Code**. Codex and other supported agents can read `AGENTS.md`; that alone does not make them execute these hooks. - **Approval:** selected consequential commands, rule-file writes and check bypasses. - **Blocking:** recognized commits containing selected secret patterns; selected final-claim contradictions, once per session per contradiction. - **Reminders and advice:** contextual guidance, hidden shell failures and weaker evidence about final claims. - **Configuration checks:** missing enforcers, generated-file drift and entry-card size. Dead routes and weaker-than-declared coverage produce warnings. The written principles are broader than the detectors. For example, an ordinary `git push`, normal `terraform apply`, and arbitrary migration or deployment scripts do not trigger the built-in irreversible-command guard. Only `block`, `ask` and `check` count toward enforced coverage. The report uses recognized repository configuration; it does not prove that a host ran a hook, that an agent followed a reminder, or that every action described by a principle is covered. Read warnings even when `check` passes. Both the graph and `check --json` name the coverage `basis` as `declared_repository_configuration`. Their `not_evaluated` list includes task completeness, undeclared requirements and live hook execution. The text report states the same boundary before its verdict. A response can obey every declared prohibition while omitting a requested issue; a configuration pass does not certify that the task is complete. Add a separate task-specific acceptance check when an omission must prevent delivery. Hooks recognize selected patterns, can be bypassed, and fail open on internal errors. They do not provide host isolation, access control or complete secret detection. See [hook details and limits](docs/maintainers/hooks.md). ## Repository map | Source | Purpose | |---|---| | [doctrine.toml](doctrine.toml) | Editable reference rules and their sources. | | [safety.py](safety.py), [doctrine.py](doctrine.py) | Setup, generation, checks and the local map server. | | [hooks.py](hooks.py), [hooks/](hooks/) | Claude Code event handlers and plugin wiring. | | [viewer/map.html](viewer/map.html) | Self-contained viewer. | | [examples/](examples/) | Sample project and synthetic hook demonstration. | | [tests/](tests/) | Checks for setup, generation, hooks and reported coverage. | | [sources/](sources/) | Attributed source excerpts and their local mappings. | | [docs/](docs/README.md) | `guides/` for adoption, `reference/` for formats and foundations, `maintainers/` for design and hooks. | | [scripts/](scripts/) | Repository checks, map review fixtures and viewer regressions. | | [skills/repository-organization/](skills/repository-organization/) | Project folder roles and staged-content checks. | ## Videos and related projects | Film | Status | What it introduces | |---|---|---| | [Introduction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uO2lbstEH9M) | Public | The wider Plectis project and its tools for inspecting agent work. | | [Safety Core walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CY4A1aEPCGc) | Public | Following a rule to files, reading its configured checks and changing a hook mode. | Both films are public on YouTube. ### Where Safety Core fits Plectis is Will Cook’s programme of research and software built with AI agents. The aim is to make the resulting work understandable enough for other people to inspect, question and build on. Safety Core contributes editable rules and checks for coding agents. - [One Checkout](https://github.com/wcook04/one-checkout) helps agents commit one reviewed patch while preserving other unfinished edits. - [Plectis toolkit](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis) contains earlier Python components and worked examples; its [software map](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/docs/system-map.html) explains their roles. - [Plectis Erdős](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos) publishes the mathematical research, proofs and open questions; [read the papers](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/maths/). Explore the [research corpus](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos) and the [Plectis website](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/). For fixes and rule proposals, see [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md). Use the [private reporting route](SECURITY.md) for vulnerabilities. ## Foundations and reuse [Constitution source notes](sources/anthropic-constitution/README.md) connect selected ideas to local principles and mechanisms. [GitHub Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit) provides a precedent for editable project constitutions. [Rulesync](https://github.com/dyoshikawa/rulesync) provides cross-tool generation; `build --export rulesync` already exports its rule format, with downstream generation a separate step. The [foundations guide](docs/reference/foundations.md) covers research, reusable skills, external guards and attribution. Safety Core is independently implemented and is not currently a Spec Kit extension. ## More detail - [Adoption and customization](docs/guides/adoption.md) - [Research and reusable foundations](docs/reference/foundations.md) - [Agent setup guide](docs/guides/agent-setup.md) - [Design](docs/maintainers/design.md), [map guide](docs/guides/map.md), [graph format](docs/reference/graph-schema.md) - Tests: `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` - Repository placement: `python3 scripts/check_repository_structure.py` (also runs in CI) - `make check` also runs viewer checks with Node.js and its built-in modules. The [bundled `safety-core` skill](skills/safety-core/SKILL.md) routes Claude Code plugin users to the [agent setup guide](docs/guides/agent-setup.md). Use either plugin hooks or per-project hooks to avoid duplicate execution. The older `doctrine.py` command and `.doctrine/` filenames remain compatible. Code: [MIT](LICENSE). The Constitution is CC0; other source references and reuse notes are recorded in the rulebook. Safety Core is not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic, OpenAI or the upstream projects cited here. ## Maintaining the tree The [directory role policy](docs/maintainers/repository-layout.json) preserves root interfaces, source homes and documented compatibility exceptions. The [organisation skill](skills/repository-organization/SKILL.md) explains changes; CI checks placements and required agent/validation routes. From the repository root: ```sh python3 skills/repository-organization/scripts/check_layout.py --config docs/maintainers/repository-layout.json python3 skills/repository-organization/scripts/test_check_layout.py ``` After staging owned changes, add `--index` to the first command to check the staged policy and staged route contents. Ignored build outputs are outside this inventory. Custom folders are welcome: declare their purpose in `docs/maintainers/repository-layout.json`. Undeclared folders produce a warning; declared placement rules still apply. See the [organisation workflow](skills/repository-organization/SKILL.md) for adding folders and generalising useful local lessons.

readme.text: # Plectis Zenith **Work in progress.** A research testbed for model-proposed experiments, measured code repair and reusable tests. Zenith investigates whether retaining programs and their supporting experiments improves performance on subsequent tasks. We evaluate model-driven program repair, reuse of generated testers, and continuation learning separately. The host executes proposed queries against candidate and reference programs, records observations, and evaluates repairs before freezing them for later tests. The current prototype can repair programs and reuse generated testers. **It has not yet shown that its retained investigation code outperforms ordinary reusable code or fixed tests.** Language-model weights stay fixed; learning here means changing the retained code, tests or state representation. The longer-term ambition is to improve the procedure that produces future improvements. That remains a research question. **[Read the paper on the web →](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-zenith/)** [Three-page paper (PDF)](paper/zenith.pdf) · [Paper source](paper/zenith.tex) · [Results and limits](docs/status.md) · [Future directions](#what-we-want-to-find-out) · [Try it locally](#try-it-without-an-account) ## What works today The paper reports separate studies and diagnostics. The continuation learner is an authored algorithm; it does not power the model-generated testers. | Experiment | Observed result | What the comparison tells us | |---|---|---| | [Reusable SQLite testers](docs/studies/client/client-investigation-v2-low-20261015.md) | Generated code found **3 of 4 authored faults**, with no model calls on the later clients. | Ordinary reusable code tied it; fixed tests found **4 of 4**. Both generated testers repeat a constant query and ignore feedback. | | [Native program repair](docs/studies/native/progress-campaign-20261014.md) | A repair call alone improved later answers from **259/576 to 365/576**. | None of the extra investigation methods beat repair alone. The twelve parent episodes cover only three authored contracts. | | [Continuation learner repair](examples/continuation-memory/witness-preserving-v1/README.md) | Restoring the paired history/test requirement lets all **8 native configurations** finish fitting. | Generic questions cost slightly less: **11,379 vs 11,395** source executions. Later UTF-8 and SQLite checks still find errors. | | [Earlier controlled question memory](docs/history/continuation-memory.md) | Retaining acquired questions reduced additional queries by **11.2–63.1%**, with the same cached answers in both conditions. | Total joint learning still cost **5,427–5,698** source executions versus **3,071** for separate ordinary modules. Blind question transfer later hurt five of six targets. | The working client run used DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: **46 calls, $0.00712** reported inference cost, including acquisition and compilation. The separate native diagnostic used Ling3.1Flash: **130 calls, $0.12983**. These are recorded run costs, not current price quotes. Qualification and earlier attempts remain in their linked reports. These are constructed, inspected workloads. They establish working mechanisms and reproducible limits; they do not establish independent transfer, a general learning advantage or recursive self-improvement. [![The implemented repair loop: measured feedback, development selection and frozen held-out evaluation](paper/repair-loop.svg)](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-zenith/) *The [website](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-zenith/) presents the paper in web form, with the same technical terms, table, citations and repair-loop diagram. The [paper guide](paper/README.md) links the PDF, source and reproductions.* Agents can read the site without JavaScript or an account: [llms.txt](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-zenith/llms.txt) gives the starting points, the [research and graph map](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-zenith/agent-map.md) explains the records, and the [machine route index](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-zenith/agent-index.json) lists their URLs. Graph records name program steps and inputs; source checksums identify versions, not scientific validity. ## How it works 1. **Propose a question.** The model sees the task, candidate program, examples and measurements available to its condition. 2. **Measure the answer.** The host executes the candidate and reference software separately. Their disagreement supplies evidence; a model's explanation does not certify the cause. 3. **Repair and check.** A replacement must preserve every previously correct measured case. Selection freezes before later evaluation. 4. **Test reuse separately.** The client study compiles a tester from earlier investigations, freezes it, and compares it with ordinary code, fresh investigation and fixed tests on later clients. Lab, Oracle and Evolve name the execution, review and revision roles. A graph can organize their dependencies; the current studies use ordinary programs and tests. The [programme](program.md) explains the graph ambition, the separate learner and their still-unbuilt connections. ## What remains open The next useful result would be a procedure that learns to choose **new, informative tests** on changed software, finds more faults or uses less work than competent ordinary testing, and repays its acquisition cost. That needs independently sourced clients with genuine room to improve, a frozen selection rule, and comparisons that include failed attempts and all stages of work. Reusing a successful probe is a starting point, not that result. One proposed engineering step is to execute and refine generated testers on development cases before freezing them. Both the retained-procedure and ordinary-code conditions would receive the same refinement allowance, with the current one-shot preparation kept as a control. Target outcomes would remain unavailable during preparation. This would first test delivery and avoidance of repeated queries; useful learning would still need a separate comparison on later clients. The [programme](program.md#how-to-choose-the-next-experiment) gives the proposed controls. ## What we want to find out Can experience help a system discover **what needs to change**, then improve how it makes the next improvement? A wrong answer might come from discarding necessary history, ignoring information already retained, or never asking the question that would reveal the problem. Those need different interventions. Zenith's records contain examples of these distinctions; they do not show that it reliably diagnoses them on its own. One possible connection is to retain the experiment that exposed a missing distinction, the histories and outcomes that justify it, the revised program, and a way to recognise when a similar investigation might help elsewhere. The separate continuation learner already represents state through answers to selected future questions. Connecting that mechanism to model-generated investigations, and making reuse selective and economical, remains future work. This is also a possible route toward **recursive self-improvement**: an improved procedure helps produce subsequent improvements. First test whether an acquired improver helps fresh problems. Hold each improver fixed while it edits untouched copies of identical, valid starting solvers. Select its proposed solver using development evidence only, freeze that solver's source hash, then evaluate it on withheld cases. Keep the evaluator outside the editable code and count acquisition, failed proposals, evaluation, execution and human intervention. Only after demonstrating a useful improver should a later experiment test whether reinvesting it produces a better successor at matched total cost. Any positive result would remain bounded by the tested tasks and budgets. The relevant methods are already established. [Predictive state representations (2001)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2001/file/1e4d36177d71bbb3558e43af9577d70e-Paper.pdf) describe stochastic state through probabilities of future tests; the cited construction assumes a known model. Zenith's separate learner instead uses an **observation table**, whose rows are access histories and whose columns are future tests, or distinguishing continuations. Its [weighted-automata antecedent](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/james.worrell/MA-learning.pdf) requires counterexample refinement to retain both the new access history and its distinguishing continuation. Our repair restores that established requirement. Agreement on the finite challenges used here does not prove equivalence to the source on every input. For testing, [ILF (CCS 2019)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3319535.3363230) trains a neural testing policy from symbolic-execution demonstrations. [CoverUp (2025, v4)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16218v4) uses an authored driver to refine generated regression tests with source coverage and execution errors. [Voyager (2023, v2)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291v2) retains and composes an executable skill library within a fixed acquisition procedure. [STOP (COLM 2024, v3)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02304v3) recursively improves a code-improvement scaffold. [Hyperagents (2026, v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19461v1) makes task-agent and meta-agent code editable and tests acquired improvement procedures in new domains. Its stronger compounding comparison remains statistically unresolved. These methods supply distinct precedents; they have not been reproduced as Zenith results. Our candidate contribution is the specific connection between measured distinctions, representation changes and better subsequent investigation. Its originality and value still need to be established against these neighbours and strong simple baselines. The [reviewed source records](paper/references.json) retain the exact editions, claim locators and limits used in the paper. ### Why connect this with mathematics? The [Plectis mathematical corpus](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos) contains papers, Lean proofs, partial results and open obligations. Its [argument-continuation exporter](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/main/scripts/export_argument_continuations.lean) looks for theorems that could supply a required hypothesis and records remaining obligations. That suggests concrete decisions to study: try to prove a prerequisite, seek a different route, or look for a counterexample. [Plectis Atlas](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-atlas) offers a complementary reading route through OpenAI's mathematics release and attributed outside assessments. The mathematics and those assessments belong to their named authors. These projects could supply problems, candidate arguments and evidence to inspect. They are **not yet connected to Zenith as a demonstrated learning system**. Finished proofs and paper collections do not supply complete records of alternative attempts or their costs. We would need records of what was known, which action was tried, its measured outcome, its cost and whether it helped the target, with solution material withheld from evaluation tasks. Lean checks a supplied proof; it does not tell us whether an unproved statement is false or whether a proposed lemma is worth pursuing. A failed search is not a negative truth label. Correct auxiliary results count as progress only when their relevance is established. Cheap software experiments are the practical first test; mathematics is a possible harder transfer domain, not a settled pivot. ### Collaboration and guidance I'm building Zenith with AI coding agents and learning the research methods as I go. This is an ambitious target, and I have limited experience in this area. The account here is my current understanding, open to correction. I'd welcome collaboration and guidance on the closest prior work, fair evaluations, useful real software tasks, or whether this mathematics connection makes sense. Small reproductions, stronger baselines and reasons a proposed approach will fail are useful contributions too. [Open an issue](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-zenith/issues) or start with the [contribution guide](CONTRIBUTING.md). ## Try it without an account Use Python 3.11 or newer from a source checkout on Linux, macOS or a suitable WSL environment. The runtime uses POSIX facilities. The examples below make no model calls. ```sh git clone https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-zenith.git cd plectis-zenith python3 -m venv .venv . .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install -e '.[test,research]' ``` **Replay the published client result:** ```sh python scripts/build_client_investigation_report.py replay-behavior examples/conformance/client-reuse-v2-low ``` A successful run reports `behavioral_match`: the archived prompts, replies, queries, outcomes, work counters and costs agree. It reports the archived and local SQLite versions; changed behavior still fails. The [strict replay](docs/studies/client/client-investigation-v2-low-20261015.md#evidence-and-replay) also requires the original runtime identity. Replay checks recorded work; it does not ask a model to solve the tasks again. **Run the separate learner example:** ```sh python scripts/demo_continuation_learning.py ``` Expect ten source calls, five rational-linear coordinates and correct outputs for queue lengths 0–32. This small example uses only the Python standard library. A single nonlinear counter solves it more simply. Add `--native` to reproduce the eight-configuration diagnostic and its residual errors. For the website, install Node.js 22.12 or newer, then run: ```sh npm ci --prefix site npm run build --prefix site python -m zenith serve --port 4175 --frontend-dir site/dist ``` Open [localhost:4175](http://localhost:4175). The public-mode server exposes published evidence, with no model-execution endpoint or private saved runs. [Frontend guide](site/README.md). ## Source map | Area | Start here | |---|---| | Current experiments | [Native repair](research/conformance_study.py), [client test reuse](research/client_investigation_study.py), [continuation learner](research/continuation_learning.py) | | Shared execution | [Restricted Python](zenith/investigation_program.py), [provider budgets](zenith/budgeted.py), [model policy](zenith/provider_policy.py), [source snapshots](zenith/source_snapshot.py) | | Evidence and replay | [Published bundles](examples/conformance), [learner example](examples/continuation-memory/witness-preserving-v1), [report/replay commands](scripts) | | Reading surfaces | [Paper](paper/README.md), [current status](docs/status.md), [website source](site/README.md), [manuscript-to-web projection](zenith/paper_reading.py) | | Paper publication | [Reviewed source records](paper/references.json), [bibliography and support checker](scripts/build_paper_references.py), [figure builder](scripts/build_paper_reading.py), [citation regressions](tests/test_paper_references.py) | | Retained graph and earlier studies | [Historical architecture and source owners](docs/history/architecture.md) | The [architecture guide](docs/architecture.md) maps dependencies, command owners and evidence boundaries. Runtime and study entry points remain stable; it also documents the retired unused tools and the documentation migration. ## Development ```sh make validate # source layout, custody and retained graph contracts make test-current # current experiments and shared execution regressions make test # complete suite, including historical studies ``` `make demo` and `make replay` run the two offline examples above. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for frontend checks and how to publish a new experiment. Useful contributions include stronger ordinary baselines, independently sourced client tasks, clearer failure reproductions and cheaper experiments with the same controls. New inference runs require an explicit command, your own credentials and a declared budget. Model selection favors recent, capable, inexpensive Chinese-developed models with verified endpoint prices; there is no automatic expensive fallback. [Run protocol](docs/studies/native/conformance-study.md#reproduce-or-run) · [Security and execution limits](SECURITY.md). ## Credits and license Created by Will Cook with AI coding agents. Zenith adapts the `ai_workflow` research system and attributed research-return components; [NOTICE](NOTICE) records their provenance. [Apache 2.0](LICENSE) covers the software. Dataset and provider-response rights are separate. The website's [reuse notes](site/README.md#what-came-from-the-original-zenith-ui) credit its components and fonts. ## Related Plectis projects - The [mathematical research corpus](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos), with papers, Lean proofs and open questions. - [Plectis Atlas](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-atlas), an independent reader for OpenAI's mathematics release and attributed external assessments. - The earlier [Plectis toolkit](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis), with reusable Python components and worked examples. - [One Checkout](https://github.com/wcook04/one-checkout), a tool for committing one reviewed patch from shared work. Will Cook uses AI agents to pursue research and build software, then prepares the results with explanations, source and checks so other people can understand, inspect and continue the work. Explore the [research corpus](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos) and [Plectis website](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/). Each repository has its own setup and evidence limits.

readme.text:
# Plectis **Tools for making AI-assisted research easier to inspect and continue.** Plectis is a public Python toolkit with programs and worked examples for checking proofs, testing records of agent actions, comparing forecasts and keeping generated documents consistent with their sources. [**Explore the system map →**](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/docs/system-map.html)
Components around the rim; the doctrine they cite at the centre. Select a component or rule on the website to follow its connections. You can run the examples independently, study how they work and adapt useful parts. The tools come from a larger research workbench built by Will Cook with AI coding agents. [Authorship, third-party sources and licensing](#name-and-history) are recorded below. > **Looking for the mathematics?** Start with > [**Plectis Erdős →**](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos), the main research > repository for the Lean proofs, papers and open questions. > [Read the guide](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/main/docs/READING_GUIDE.md) > or [explore the mathematics map](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/maths/universe.html). [Worked examples](#see-it-work) · [Quickstart](QUICKSTART.md) · [Documentation](docs/README.md) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) Browse the live [component pages](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/docs/components.html), [papers](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/#papers) and [films](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/#videos) on the [Plectis website](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/). The website and its maps are agent-readable. Start with the [agent navigation guide](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/llms.txt) for text indexes, graph data and source links without running the visual maps. For a first look in a terminal, run the repository tour. Two commands, no install, Python 3.11 or newer: ```bash git clone https://github.com/wcook04/plectis && cd plectis PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m plectis tour --format text . ``` This lists project files, suggests a starting task and saves a local run record. It makes no model calls and leaves your source unchanged. The examples below show what the individual tools do; the tour itself does not run your tests or carry out the suggested task. ## Why this exists AI-assisted research can span many sessions, files and failed approaches. Plectis explores how to preserve that work so another person can understand what was tried, check the results and choose a useful next step. Experts can contribute a correction or direction without operating the AI themselves. This toolkit publishes selected parts of that effort. The [mathematics repository](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos) contains the papers, proofs and open questions; the [website](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/) explains both. The larger private workbench shown in the videos is separate from this clone. The [project overview](docs/overview.md) explains how the parts fit together and relates them to other research tools. ## Choose a starting point | You want to… | Start here | |---|---| | Understand the project | [Why these tools belong together](docs/overview.md) | | Run something locally | [Quickstart](QUICKSTART.md) | | Follow a complete example | [Worked guides](docs/guides/README.md) | | Find a tool in your field | [Component map](ORGANS.md) | | Work on the code | [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [implementation map](docs/maintainers/architecture.md#implementation-map) | | Read the mathematics | [Companion reader's guide](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/main/docs/READING_GUIDE.md) | ## See it work An AI says: “I committed the fix and the tests passed.” The [completion-checking guide](docs/guides/checking-agent-completion.md) shows how one component checks those claims using a sample Git repository and actual pytest runs. It verifies three supplied claims and rejects four deliberately incorrect ones. You can follow the result back to the code that checked it. Two more [worked guides](docs/guides/README.md) show different uses: - [Change a prompt-injection example](docs/guides/prompt-injection.md) and see a checker reject an inconsistent permission in saved records. - [Prepare a research question](docs/guides/hypothesis-handoffs.md) with a tentative answer, alternatives and proposed observations for an expert. Try the second example from the clone, without installing anything: ```bash PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m plectis hypothesis-handoff \ --input examples/hypothesis_handoff/independent_evaluation.json --format text ``` It validates the supplied file and prints the question and proposed investigation. It does not answer the question, contact an expert or call a model. Each guide explains what its example tests and what remains untested. ## What is in the toolkit? There are **88 components**, grouped into seven areas. A component is a named program or group of related programs, with its own instructions and stated limits. Some run a computation or an external tool; others compare supplied records against rules. An entry in the catalogue is not a promise that every example can run in every environment: its page lists required tools and source files, and the runner reports unavailable requirements. | Area | Try it for… | |---|---| | [Entry and orientation](ORGANS.md#entry--reveal) | Checking that a suggested first step names an available command and result file. | | [Architecture and navigation](ORGANS.md#architecture--navigation) | Comparing a selection of files and components with an expected selection. | | [Mathematics and proof](ORGANS.md#formal-math--proof) | Trying proof steps on supplied theorems and asking Lean to check them. | | [Agent reliability and safety](ORGANS.md#agent-reliability--safety-replays) | Testing records of prompt injection, poisoned memory or completion claims. | | [Research and forecasting](ORGANS.md#research--science-replays) | Comparing forecast errors on synthetic data. | | [Source and generated files](ORGANS.md#import-projection--drift) | Comparing file fingerprints and checking that declared outputs exist. | | [Work and continuity](ORGANS.md#work-landing--continuity) | Checking that a work record names its changes, validation results and commits. | You can [browse the components on the website](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis/docs/components.html) or list and search their descriptions from the terminal: ```bash PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m plectis comprehend --slice mechanism --format text PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m plectis comprehend --first-action "prompt injection" --format text ``` The search uses phrase and word matching to suggest a command and relevant files. It neither calls an AI model nor executes the suggested command. ## How it works Most components run independently. They share command handling, file formats and a catalogue that names each component's code, inputs, checks and saved results. The catalogue also supplies the generated documentation and maps. The connections between components are recorded where they exist; the seven areas are a browsing aid, not seven stages that every run executes. To understand a component, open its example input, the source function that processes it and the output it produces. Compare that output with the test or expected result. Then change an input in a disposable copy and check whether the result changes as expected. The [worked guide](docs/guides/prompt-injection.md) follows this path through one component. The project tour is a separate orientation command. It mostly classifies filenames and paths, with limited inspection of Python entry points. It writes a file inventory, suggested tasks and a simulated task record under `.microcosm/`, an ignored directory retained from the project's former name. A saved run result is called a *receipt* in the source. It records what ran and which inputs and results it refers to; it does not by itself prove a claim. To see the tour's structured output: ```bash PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m plectis tour --card . ``` [Architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md) maps the implementation. The [maintainer guides](docs/maintainers/README.md) explain command dispatch, data ownership and how to regenerate the maps. ## Explore with a coding agent A coding agent is an AI assistant that can read files, run commands and edit code. You can use your own to explore this repository. Open a current clone and ask, for example: > Read AGENTS.override.md. I want to understand how this project checks an > agent's claim that a task is finished. Find the relevant example, explain > its inputs, run it, and show me the result and the code that checks it. > Explain what this run establishes and what it leaves untested. Include the > checkout commit and commands so I can repeat it. The [agent quickstart](QUICKSTART.md#use-your-own-coding-agent) explains where to save results. [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) contains the editing instructions. The toolkit's local examples do not require a model API key; your chosen coding agent has its own account and provider requirements. ## Install The basic commands run from a clone with **Python 3.11 or newer**, without third-party runtime dependencies. The shell examples above work on macOS, Linux and WSL. In Windows PowerShell, first set `$env:PYTHONPATH = 'src'`, then use `python -m plectis` in place of `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m plectis`. Individual examples may require Git, pytest, Lean or other tools; follow the selected example's instructions. To install the shorter `plectis` command on macOS or Linux: ```bash python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install . .venv/bin/plectis tour --format text . ``` Use the virtual environment if your system Python reports [`externally-managed-environment`](https://peps.python.org/pep-0668/). For development dependencies, Windows installation commands and other options, see [Quickstart](QUICKSTART.md), [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [troubleshooting](docs/README.md#troubleshooting). The older `microcosm` command remains an alias. ## Repository layout Start with the guides and examples. The large reference files are indexes for looking things up; you do not need to read them all before trying a component. ```text plectis/ ├── src/ │ ├── plectis/ Public command entry points │ └── microcosm_core/ Python implementation; components in organs/ ├── docs/ Guides, reference, maintainer notes and paper guide ├── examples/ Runnable examples and checked source bundles ├── fixtures/ Prepared inputs and expected results ├── tests/ Executable checks ├── core/ Component registry and configuration ├── atlas/ Generated maps and indexes ├── standards/ Requirements checked by the tools ├── skills/ Procedures for agents ├── paper_modules/ Component explanations ├── paper/ Toolkit paper source ├── receipts/ Recorded example results ├── assets/ README and social preview images └── scripts/ ├── build/ Documentation and map generators ├── check/ Source, projection and boundary checks ├── release/ Packaging and release verification ├── inspect/ Compact inspection cards └── papers/ Publication corpus tools ``` Start with the [examples](examples/README.md); use the [fixtures](fixtures/README.md) and [recorded results](receipts/README.md) to understand their checks. Your own runs go in the ignored `.microcosm/` directory. The [paper guide](docs/papers/README.md) distinguishes the toolkit paper's [source](paper/README.md) from the main research papers. The root `ORGANS.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md` and `AGENT_ROUTES.md` are generated indexes. `AXIOMS.md`, `PRINCIPLES.md` and `ANTI_PRINCIPLES.md` contain the [doctrine shown in the map](docs/reference/README.md#the-doctrine-in-the-map). `Makefile` and `.github/workflows/` run the checks. The [maintainer architecture guide](docs/maintainers/architecture.md) identifies which files to edit and which builders to run. The [script guide](scripts/README.md) explains each maintenance role; `make check` enforces their placement in Git and CI. The [documentation index](docs/README.md) separates human guides, reference maps and maintainer instructions. Directory READMEs explain the examples and reference collections. The [terminology guide](docs/reference/terminology.md) translates older names you may encounter in source files. ## What a passing result means A pass is about a particular input and check. The component records classify the result: a computation run now, a replay of supplied data, or a comparison of files. That is why the source, test and stated limits are published together.
Limits by kind of example - **Formal proof:** Lean can check the supplied formal statement and proof. A successful toolkit example does not prove an unrelated theorem. - **Agent safety:** a replay does not establish that a deployed agent is safe. Its prepared cases cover specific checks, not every possible attack. - **Research and forecasting:** synthetic examples do not establish scientific expertise, investment returns or a forecasting track record. This is not professional advice or investment advice. - **Generated files:** a match establishes agreement for the specified files. You do not gain permission to publish private material by comparing them. - **Recording and resuming work:** you do not gain permission to edit someone else's source files or publish a release by recording a task as complete.
This is a research prototype containing selected public source files and examples. It does not contain enough code or data to reconstruct the private system.
