papers.title: Reciprocal Sums and the Sylvester Recurrence: Further Results and Proofs

sections: The two remaining cubics fail modulo seven
Polynomial extraction at a regular rate
Zero errors and the Sylvester recurrence
Bounds that allow for cancellation and earlier decreases
Counting jumps before a prime power can be lost
Bounds on the error and on the original sequence
Signs of the error and of the growth ratio
Growth of the factors repeated in the denominator
A factorial modulus for integral recursion

excerpts.text:
We study rational reciprocal sums with $a_{n+1}/a_n^2\to1$.
Integer finite differences exclude nonintegral regular rates and reduce
the cubic rate to a polynomial. A square condition in the cubic field
and congruences modulo seven then prove irrationality.
For general rational tails, we derive Sylvester recurrence criteria
from persistent divisors, bounded numerator increases and weighted
crossings of new maxima. We describe the arithmetic estimates still
needed for Erd\H{o}s Problem~\#243.

\section{Introduction}\label{long243:sec:problem}
Sylvester's sequence $2,3,7,43,1807,\ldots$ has reciprocal sum $1$.
Its recurrence $a_n=a_{n-1}^2-a_{n-1}+1$ gives the telescoping identity
\[
 \frac1{a_{n-1}-1}=\frac1{a_{n-1}}+\frac1{a_n-1}.
\]
The tail beginning with $1/a_{n-1}$ therefore equals $1/(a_{n-1}-1)$.
Erd\H{o}s Problem~\#243 asks whether every rational reciprocal sum
with $a_n\sim a_{n-1}^2$ must eventually have this form:

\begin{problem}[Erd\H{o}s \#243]\label{long243:res:problem}
Let $1\le a_1<a_2<\cdots$ be a sequence of integers with
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}^{2}}=1
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \sum\frac{1}{a_n}\in\Q .
\]
Then $a_n=a_{n-1}^{2}-a_{n-1}+1$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
\end{problem}

\noindent See~\cite[p.~64]{erdosgraham1980} and~\cite[p.~105]{erdos1988}.
Bloom's catalogue, accessed 28 July 2026, lists the problem as
open~\cite{erdosproblems}.
Below we index the same recurrence as
$a_{n+1}=a_n^{2}-a_n+1$, which is the shift the formal sources use; the two
forms are the same statement. The polynomial $a^2-a+1$ is called the
\lword{Erdos243/ReciprocalTailRigidity.lean}{37}{sylvesterNext}{Sylvester
successor}.

Clearing a rational reciprocal tail gives positive integers $C_n,D_n$
with $C_{n+1}=a_nC_n-D_n$ and $D_{n+1}=a_nD_n$. The first update
can also be written $C_{n+1}=C_n-E_n$, where
$E_n=D_n-(a_n-1)C_n$. Quadratic growth makes $E_n/C_n\to0$.
The eventual Sylvester recurrence follows once the integer error itself
vanishes.

There are two ways to use this integer numerator. At a precise regular
rate it grows, but a high finite difference tends to zero and must
vanish. The resulting polynomial is then tested against the denominator
recurrence. With bounded upward steps, a different argument applies:
a stable common divisor gives reduced tails, whose numerators avoid
every earlier multiplier. The Chinese remainder theorem produces a
block that bounded rises cannot cross, regardless of intervening
decreases. Neither argument replaces the denominator recurrence by a
scalar growth estimate.

Section~\ref{long243:sec:cubicrate} proves cubic and nonintegral-rate
irrationality: these rates exclude the eventual Sylvester recurrence.
The general question remains open. After the literature comparison in
Section~\ref{long243:sec:priorwork},
Sections~\ref{long243:sec:state}--\ref{long243:sec:defect} develop
integer tails and zero-error identities for the subsequent criteria.

The later criteria use two distinct normalisations.
Section~\ref{long243:sec:lcmrecords} clears tails with an LCM: common
numerator factors remain, so congruences forbid short crossings rather
than numerator values. Section~\ref{long243:sec:records} reduces to
lowest terms, where cancellation can remove a prime that persists in
the LCM. That argument must track the prime powers which survive. Sections~\ref{long243:sec:constant}--\ref{long243:sec:periodic}
treat constant and periodic errors;
Sections~\ref{long243:sec:barrier}--\ref{long243:sec:bounded} prove
the bounded-increase criterion, and Section~\ref{long243:sec:mass}
treats scalar summability. Section~\ref{long243:sec:open} separates open
estimates from countermodels to weakened hypotheses. The appendices
give formal sources, the finite residue calculation and a result map.

We use $z_+=\max(z,0)$. Deleting a finite prefix is harmless for an eventual
recurrence, but not for the coefficients in a higher-order rate. In
particular, the index $n$ in $1+3/n+o(n^{-3})$ is kept fixed throughout
the cubic proof. The recurrence sections also use zero-based indexing,
with that convention stated where the integer sequences are introduced.


\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Keywords.} irrationality; Ahmes series; Sylvester's sequence;
unit fractions; Lean~4.
\qquad
\textbf{MSC 2020.} 11J72 (primary); 11B37, 11D68, 68V20 (secondary).

excerpts.section: The two remaining cubics fail modulo seven
excerpts.text:
\subsection{The two remaining cubics fail modulo seven}\label{long243:sec:modseven}

\begin{lemma}[two incompatible four-term residue patterns]\label{long243:res:modseven}
For $Q_{12,1}$, every sufficiently late four-index window beginning at
$n\equiv0\pmod7$ contains an exceptional index. For $Q_{12,-1}$, the same
holds for windows beginning at $n\equiv1\pmod7$. In either case,
$\underline d(S)\ge1/7$.
The specified starting residue classes are part of the assertion; no
claim is made for every block of four consecutive indices.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Reduce modulo $7$.  For $c=1$ the values of $Q_{12,1}$ at $n=0,1,2,3$ are
$1,13,49,121$, that is
\begin{equation}\label{long243:eq:wordplus}
 (1,6,0,2),
\end{equation}
and for $c=-1$ the values at $n=1,2,3,4$ are $11,47,119,239$, that is
\begin{equation}\label{long243:eq:wordminus}
 (4,5,0,1).
\end{equation}
Each four-term pattern recurs with period $7$.

Index a proposed occurrence locally by $0,1,2,3$, and use $a_i$ for the
multiplier at local index $i$. Let $(c_0,c_1,0,c_3)$ be the residues of
$u$ and $(d_0,d_1,d_2,d_3)$ those of $v$. Thus
$c_{i+1}=a_ic_i-d_i$ and $d_{i+1}=a_id_i$ modulo $7$.  The middle zero gives
$a_1c_1=d_1$, then $d_2=a_1d_1$ and $c_3=-d_2$, so
\begin{equation}\label{long243:eq:d1square}
 d_1^2=c_1\,a_1d_1=c_1d_2=-c_1c_3 .
\end{equation}
For \eqref{long243:eq:wordplus} this is $-6\cdot2=2$, and for \eqref{long243:eq:wordminus} it
is $-5\cdot1=2$.  The square roots of $2$ modulo $7$ are $3$ and $4$, so
$d_1\in\{3,4\}$ in both cases.

The first step gives $a_0=(c_1+d_0)/c_0$ and hence
$d_1=d_0(d_0+c_1)/c_0$, which is legitimate because $c_0\in\{1,4\}$ is
invertible.  For \eqref{long243:eq:wordplus} this is $d_1=d_0(d_0+6)$, with values
\[
 (0,0,2,6,5,6,2) \qquad\text{at } d_0=0,1,\ldots,6,
\]
and for \eqref{long243:eq:wordminus} it is $d_1=2d_0(d_0+5)$, with values
\[
 (0,5,0,6,2,2,6).
\]
The incompatibility also follows without enumerating $d_0$. Completing
the square gives
\[
 d_1+2=(d_0+3)^2\quad(c=1),\qquad
 d_1+2=2(d_0-1)^2\quad(c=-1).
\]
Since $2$ is a square modulo $7$, either update makes $d_1+2$ a square.
The required values $d_1=3,4$ instead give the nonsquares $5,6$.
The two displayed lists provide the same exhaustive check: both images
are $\{0,2,5,6\}$, disjoint from $\{3,4\}$.

Hence every sufficiently late window $[7k,7k+3]$ for the plus profile,
and every sufficiently late window $[1+7k,4+7k]$ for the minus profile,
contains an element of $S$. Windows within each family are pairwise disjoint.
There are $X/7+O(1)$ such windows contained in $[0,X]$, so choosing one
exceptional index in each gives $\#(S\cap[0,X])\ge X/7-O(1)$ and therefore
$\underline d(S)\ge1/7$. This stronger local bound is not promoted to a
uniform lower bound for arbitrary cubic profiles.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{long243:res:cubicexclusion}]
Assume $\underline d(S)=0$.  Lemmas~\ref{long243:res:gcdshape}
and~\ref{long243:res:reduciblecase} put the primitive tail in the shape \eqref{long243:eq:Qmc}
with $c=\pm1$ and $Q_{m,c}$ irreducible.  Each excluded branch already
contradicts the assumption by producing a positive, branch-dependent lower
density, namely $1/(12\ell)$ or $1/\ell$ for the relevant prime $\ell$.
Proposition~\ref{long243:res:transportsquare} and Lemma~\ref{long243:res:scaletwelve} force
$m=12$, and Lemma~\ref{long243:res:modseven} then gives
$\underline d(S)\ge1/7$, the final contradiction.
\end{proof}

The two densities play different roles. If the field element is not
a square, Chebotarev supplies one witnessing prime; its periodic
obstruction gives a positive density of disagreement \emph{indices}.
No lower bound uniform over cubic profiles is needed.

% whose tree keeps the Lean roots under lean/.

\hypersetup{
  pdftitle={Integral relations among totient sections},
  pdfsubject={Erdős Problem Notes: Problem 249},
  pdfkeywords={irrationality, Euler totient, k-regular sequences, 2-kernel, Lambert series, Möbius inversion, linear independence, Lean 4},
}

\newtheorem{equivform}[theorem]{Equivalent formulation}


\runninghead{Integral relations among totient sections}
\title{Integral Relations among Totient Sections}
\subtitle{Finite-level bases and bounded residue series}
\author{Will Cook}
\date{July 2026; revised 1 October 2026}


% Named destinations are outside all theorem bodies.
\newcommand{\longrecord}[2]{\href{erdos249-totient-reasoning-surface.pdf\##1}{#2}}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\noteprovenance

\begin{abstract}
For integers $k\ge2$ and $e\ge1$, every totient section
$n\mapsto\varphi(k^jn+r)$ with $0\le j\le e$, $0\le r<k^j$,
is an explicit integer multiple of one of $k^e+1$ independent sections.
The resulting two-term relations form an integral basis of all relations
among the indexed sections: their coefficients are recovered without
division. Martin's stronger affine theorem gives the independence;
we also prove it directly by making an evaluation matrix diagonal
modulo a prime. The same separation method classifies rational binary
series formed from dyadic totient residues. It does not settle the
irrationality of the unreduced binary totient series.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:results}
\papersectiontarget{short249-basis}
Splitting the totient sequence into its even and odd subsequences,
then splitting once more, gives seven sequences:
\[
 \varphi(n);\qquad
 \varphi(2n),\ \varphi(2n+1);\qquad
 \varphi(4n),\ \varphi(4n+1),\ \varphi(4n+2),\ \varphi(4n+3).
\]
The identities
\[
 \varphi(4n)=2\varphi(2n),\qquad
 \varphi(4n+2)=\varphi(2n+1)
\]
leave five independent sequences. Thus every identity among the seven
comes from these two substitutions. More precisely, an integral
relation is a unique integral combination of the two displayed
relations. We will prove the same statement at every depth and in
every integer base.

For an integer $k\ge2$, the \emph{totient sections} are the sequences
$n\mapsto\varphi(k^jn+r)$, where $j\ge0$ and $0\le r<k^j$.
Throughout, $n$ ranges over $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ and
$\varphi(0)=0$. To describe relations we retain a separate index for
each pair $(j,r)$, even when two pairs give the same sequence.
For example, $\varphi(4n+2)$ and $\varphi(2n+1)$ are equal sequences
but occupy different positions in the list above.

The sections form the $k$-kernel of the totient sequence. A sequence is
$k$-regular when the $\Z$-module generated by its $k$-kernel is finitely
generated~\cite{allouche-shallit}. Coons proved that the totient sequence is
not $k$-regular for any $k\ge2$~\cite[Thm.~3.2]{coons}.
Here we determine those modules at each finite level, including their
integral relations. The theorem gives the basis and the substitutions;
Corollary~\ref{cor:integral-normal-form} explains how to recover every
relation from them. Level zero contains only $\varphi(n)$ and has
dimension one.

\begin{theorem}[A basis through each finite level]
\label{thm:kkernelrank}
Let $k\ge2$ and $e\ge1$ be integers, write $F^{(k)}_{j,r}(n)=\ph(k^jn+r)$, and put
\[
 V_{k,e}=\operatorname{span}_{\Q}
 \{\,F^{(k)}_{j,r}:0\le j\le e,\ 0\le r<k^j\,\}.
\]
Then $\dim_{\Q}V_{k,e}=k^e+1$, and
\[
 \mathcal B_{k,e}
 =\{F^{(k)}_{0,0},F^{(k)}_{1,0}\}
 \cup\{\,F^{(k)}_{j,r}:1\le j\le e,\ 1\le r<k^j,\ k\nmid r\,\}
\]
is a basis.  Every omitted section reduces to a basis element by an explicit
scalar: $F^{(k)}_{j,0}=k^{j-1}F^{(k)}_{1,0}$ for $j\ge1$, and if $r=k^tu$ with
$t=\max\{s:k^s\mid r\}\ge1$ and $k\nmid u$, then
\[
 F^{(k)}_{j,r}=C_k(t,u)\,F^{(k)}_{j-t,u},
 \qquad
 C_k(t,u)=k^t\prod_{\substack{p\mid k\\ p\nmid u}}\Bigl(1-\tfrac1p\Bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

The condition $k\nmid r$ allows residues with $\gcd(k,r)>1$.
For instance, $r=1$ and $r=2$ are both retained in base six, and the
reductions involving them are
\[
 \varphi(36n+6)=2\varphi(6n+1),\qquad
 \varphi(36n+12)=4\varphi(6n+2).
\]
The factor $2$ is already present in $6n+2$ but not in $6n+1$;
only newly introduced prime divisors contribute factors $1-1/p$.
Thus one removes whole factors of $k$ from the residue, not every
common prime factor. Repeated prime factors of $k$ cause no exception.

Martin's 2006 theorem on simultaneous totient inequalities already
implies independence for every finite family of pairwise
nonproportional affine forms with positive integral slopes
\cite[Thm.~1]{martin-phi-inequalities}. Its conclusion is stronger
than the independence used here. The point of the present description
is the explicit reduction of the sections and the integral relation
basis in Corollary~\ref{cor:integral-normal-form}.
We also give a direct proof that constructs a nonsingular evaluation
matrix. It uses the CRT--Dirichlet separation argument in Yazdani's
proof of Theorem~2, credited there to Shallit
\cite[pp.~652--653]{yazdani2001}. The step that needs care is to keep
the progression for the selected affine form reduced while imposing
prime divisors on all the others.

The proof in Section~\ref{sec:rank} separates scalar reduction from
independence. Section~\ref{sec:base-six-test} recovers the integral
relations, starting in base six. Section~\ref{sec:family} uses prime
isolation for bounded functions of totient residues.
The series
\[
 S=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\varphi(n)}{2^n}
\]
has unbounded coefficients. Its irrationality, asked in
Erd\H{o}s Problem~\#249~\cite[p.~61]{erdosgraham1980}, remains open.
The coefficient basis supplies no irrationality conclusion for this
value. Appendix~\ref{app:sources} gives further coefficient
consequences; Appendices~\ref{sec:carry-rank} and~\ref{sec:open}
collect the tail identities, comparison sequences and still-unproved
cancellation estimates relevant to $S$. Their longer proofs are in
\longrecord{long249-r3-complements}{\emph{The Binary Totient Series}}.

\section{Proof of the basis theorem}\label{sec:rank}
\papersectiontarget{short249-proof}
\subsection*{Scalar reductions}
The product formula reduces every omitted section to an integer
multiple of a retained one.
For a zero residue, $kn$ and $k^jn$ have the same prime divisors when
$n>0$. Hence
$\varphi(k^jn)=k^{j-1}\varphi(kn)$; both sides vanish at $n=0$.
For an omitted positive residue $r=k^tu$ with $t\ge1$ and $k\nmid u$,
we have $t<j$ because $0<r<k^j$. Put $m=k^{j-t}n+u$. A prime $p\mid k$ divides $m$ exactly when it divides
$u$. The product formula for $\varphi(k^tm)/\varphi(m)$ therefore
contributes $k^t$ and one factor $1-1/p$ for each prime $p\mid k$
absent from $u$. The multiplier is an integer: its denominator is a
product of distinct primes dividing $k$, and therefore divides $k^t$.
This gives $C_k(t,u)$ and proves that the stated family spans $V_{k,e}$.

\subsection*{Affine independence}
Independence follows from Martin's theorem. For any ordering of
pairwise nonproportional affine forms and any $C>0$, it gives a set
of positive lower density on which each successive totient ratio
exceeds $C$. In a proposed nonzero relation, place a nonzero
coefficient $c_1$ first and take
$C>\max(1,\sum_{i>1}|c_i|/|c_1|)$. The first term then dominates
the sum of all remaining terms in absolute value, a contradiction
\cite[Thm.~1]{martin-phi-inequalities}. This also proves independence
after any finite prefix is deleted.

The direct proof isolates one column in each evaluation row. Let
$L_i(n)=a_i n+b_i$ for $1\le i\le s$, where $a_i>0$ and
$a_i b_j-a_j b_i\ne0$ for $i\ne j$. Shift $n$ so that all $b_i$
are positive; the cross determinants do not change. Write
$L_i=g_iA_i$, where $g_i=\gcd(a_i,b_i)$ and $A_i$ is primitive.
We make $A_i$, not $L_i$, prime: $L_i$ may have the fixed divisor
$g_i>1$. We seek a prime $\ell$ and points $n_1,\ldots,n_s$ for which
\begin{equation}\label{eq:diagonal-evaluation}
 E=\bigl(\varphi(L_j(n_i))\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le s}
 \equiv
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \varphi(g_1)&0&\cdots&0\\
 0&\varphi(g_2)&\cdots&0\\
 \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
 0&0&\cdots&\varphi(g_s)
 \end{pmatrix}\pmod\ell,
 \qquad \ell\nmid\prod_i\varphi(g_i).
\end{equation}
Since $\det E\not\equiv0\pmod\ell$, $E$ is invertible over $\Q$.
A rational relation gives $Ec=0$, hence $c=0$. We now construct
the rows.

For $j\ne i$, a prime divisor $q_{ij}\equiv1\pmod\ell$ of
$L_j(n_i)$ makes $\ell\mid q_{ij}-1\mid\varphi(L_j(n_i))$.
For the diagonal entry, we instead make $A_i(n_i)$ prime and
congruent to $2$ modulo $\ell$.
Choose an odd $\ell$ dividing none of the slopes $a_i$, the products
$g_i\varphi(g_i)$ or the nonzero cross determinants. For each fixed
$i$, Dirichlet's theorem supplies distinct primes
$q_{ij}\equiv1\pmod\ell$ ($j\ne i$) outside the same finite exceptional
set. Impose
\[
 A_i(n)\equiv2\pmod\ell,\qquad
 L_j(n)\equiv0\pmod{q_{ij}}\quad(j\ne i).
\]
Each congruence is soluble because its slope is coprime to its
modulus. CRT combines them into $n=n_0+Ru$, where
$R=\ell\prod_{j\ne i}q_{ij}$.

CRT supplies the congruences, but not yet a prime value. Dirichlet
applies to the progression of values of $A_i$, namely
\[
 A_i(n_0+Ru)=A_i(n_0)+(a_i/g_i)Ru.
\]
Its initial value must be coprime to its step. The step has only
three kinds of prime factors: those of $a_i/g_i$, excluded by
primitivity; $\ell$, excluded by the residue $2$; and the imposed
$q_{ij}$. Such a $q_{ij}$ cannot divide
$A_i(n_0)$: it would then divide both $L_i(n_0)$ and $L_j(n_0)$, hence
\[
 a_iL_j(n_0)-a_jL_i(n_0)=a_i b_j-a_j b_i,
\]
contrary to its choice. This is where nonproportionality is used:
the nonzero cross determinant lets us keep each imposed divisor
away from the selected form. We may now choose $p=A_i(n_i)$ prime,
as large as needed,
and in particular with $p\nmid g_i$. Then
\[
 \varphi(L_i(n_i))=\varphi(g_i)(p-1)
       \equiv\varphi(g_i)\not\equiv0\pmod\ell,
\]
while all the other entries of row $i$ vanish modulo $\ell$.
We choose the rows separately, applying Dirichlet's theorem once
more for each selected form $A_i$. Thus no simultaneous primality
assertion is required. The construction proves
\eqref{eq:diagonal-evaluation} with every $n_i$ beyond any prescribed
threshold.

\subsection*{The two zero-residue sections}
The arguments $n,kn$ are proportional; their totient sequences are
not. We first merge their coefficients on
$n=km+1$, where $\varphi(kn)=\varphi(k)\varphi(n)$, then separate
them using a different ratio. On this progression the
positive-residue sections have arguments
\[
 k^{j+1}m+k^j+r\quad(k\nmid r),
\]
together with $km+1$. These are pairwise nonproportional: equality of
two intercept-to-slope ratios would give
$r/k^j=r'/k^{j'}$, which for $j'>j$ forces $k\mid r'$.
No positive-residue form is proportional to $km+1$.
If $A,B$ multiply $\varphi(n),\varphi(kn)$, affine independence
therefore leaves $A+B\varphi(k)=0$ and eliminates every other
coefficient. At $n=k$, however, the ratio is $k$, giving $A+Bk=0$.
Since $\varphi(k)<k$, these two equations separate the remaining
coefficients: $A=B=0$. Finally,
\[
 \lvert\mathcal B_{k,e}\rvert
   =2+\sum_{j=1}^e(k^j-k^{j-1})=k^e+1,
\]
which completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:kkernelrank}.
For independence on a tail, use a sufficiently large power of $k$
in the last evaluation.

\section{Integral relations}\label{sec:base-six-test}
\papersectiontarget{short249-base-six}
Independence turns identities into coordinate calculations. In base six
at level two, the $43$ indexed sections reduce to $37$ retained ones:
$F_{0,0},F_{1,0}$, the five
$F_{1,r}$ ($1\le r\le5$), and the $30$ sections $F_{2,r}$ with
$1\le r<36$ and $6\nmid r$. The omitted sections satisfy
\[
\begin{aligned}
 F_{2,0}&=6F_{1,0}, & F_{2,6}&=2F_{1,1}, & F_{2,12}&=4F_{1,2},\\
 F_{2,18}&=3F_{1,3}, & F_{2,24}&=4F_{1,4}, & F_{2,30}&=2F_{1,5}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The formal symbols $E_{j,r}$ remain independent even when their
sequences $F_{j,r}$ coincide. The substitution $F_{2,12}=4F_{1,2}$
corresponds to the decomposition
\[
 x_{1,2}E_{1,2}+x_{2,12}E_{2,12}
 = (x_{1,2}+4x_{2,12})E_{1,2}
   +x_{2,12}(E_{2,12}-4E_{1,2}).
\]
The retained coefficient becomes $x_{1,2}+4x_{2,12}$; the relation
coefficient is the original $x_{2,12}$. After all six substitutions,
the evaluated sequence vanishes exactly when the $37$ retained
coefficients vanish. In that case, the relation coordinates are the six
original omitted coefficients. In the opening binary example the
relation vectors are $E_{2,0}-2E_{1,0}$ and $E_{2,2}-E_{1,1}$.

\begin{corollary}[Integral coordinates and all integral relations]\label{cor:integral-normal-form}
Let $k\ge2$ and $e\ge1$. The retained family is a $\Z$-basis of the
module generated by the sections through level $e$. Index the sections
by their level and residue, retaining distinct indices even when they
define equal sequences. For each omitted index $i$, write the scalar
reduction as $F_i=a_iF_{j(i)}$, where $j(i)$ is retained and $a_i$ is a
nonnegative integer. In the free abelian group with one generator $E_i$
for each of these indices, the vectors
\[
 R_i=E_i-a_iE_{j(i)}\qquad(i\text{ omitted})
\]
form a $\Z$-basis of the kernel of evaluation $E_i\mapsto F_i$.
In particular, every integral relation has a unique integral expression
in these elementary relations, and their rank is
$\sum_{j=1}^{e-1}k^j$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Since $\prod_{p\mid k,\,p\nmid u}p$ divides $k$, every scalar
$C_k(t,u)$ is an integer. The retained family therefore spans the
section module over $\Z$, and its rational independence makes it a
$\Z$-basis.

For any vector $x=\sum_i x_iE_i$, substitute
$E_i=R_i+a_iE_{j(i)}$ at each omitted index and collect terms:
\[
 x=\sum_{j\text{ retained}}
       \left(x_j+\sum_{\substack{i\text{ omitted}\\j(i)=j}}a_i x_i\right)E_j
       +\sum_{i\text{ omitted}}x_iR_i.
\]
The first sum gives the retained coordinates of the evaluated
sequence; the second evaluates to zero. Thus $x$ is a relation
exactly when the first sum vanishes, in which case
$x=\sum_{i\text{ omitted}}x_iR_i$. This expression is unique:
at omitted index $i$, the coefficient of $\sum_h c_hR_h$ is $c_i$
itself. Each substitution has a unit coefficient at its own omitted
index, so the entire calculation takes place over $\Z$, without division.
Counting omitted indices gives
$(1+k+\cdots+k^e)-(k^e+1)=\sum_{j=1}^{e-1}k^j$.
\end{proof}
The \emph{section-generated} module need not contain every integer-valued
sequence in its rational span: for $k=2$, $e\ge2$, the sequence
$\varphi(4n+3)/2$ is integer-valued but has retained coordinate $1/2$.
This failure of saturation concerns the image of evaluation; the integral
relation basis describes the kernel.

In the same base-six example, evaluation gives a second test.
Order the retained columns as above, with residues increasing within
each level, and evaluate at $n=0,\ldots,36$ to obtain a $37\times37$ matrix.
Its determinant is $17$ modulo $101$, so it is nonsingular over $\Q$.
Consequently a retained combination is zero if and only if all $37$
of its integer evaluations are zero. Here reduction modulo $101$
certifies the matrix, not the equality of a proposed combination:
$101F_{2,2}$ would vanish modulo $101$ at every input, although its
integer value at $n=0$ is $101$.
The script \texttt{scripts/totient\_kernel\_normal\_form.py} calculates
the coordinates and the first nonzero evaluation using integer arithmetic.

\section{Bounded functions of totient residues}\label{sec:family}
\papersectiontarget{short249-residues}
The same separation method now isolates a coefficient between long
zero blocks. For bounded integer coefficients, rationality puts scaled
tails in a fixed lattice: the right block forces a tail to zero,
and the left leaves a nonzero tail of magnitude below the lattice spacing.
Residues below are least nonnegative representatives, not necessarily
binary digits.
\begin{theorem}[Series of totient residues]\label{res:residueseries}
For every $m\ge3$,
\[
 \sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\ph(n)\bmod m}{2^n}\notin\Q.
\]
For $k\ge1$ and $f:\Z/2^k\Z\to\Q$, the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}f(\ph(n)\bmod2^k)2^{-n}$ is rational exactly when $f$ is
constant on the even residue classes. If that constant is $c$, its value is
$3f(1)/4+c/4$.
\end{theorem}
Only $f(1)$ and the even classes are visible to the series:
$\varphi(1)=\varphi(2)=1$ and all later totients are even.
This explains the rational case, including the value $3/4$ modulo
two. The irrational case rests on the pattern
\[
 \underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{L\text{ terms}},\quad
 a_N\ne0,\quad
 \underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{L\text{ terms}}.
\]
The coefficients outside the window may have either sign; only their
uniform bound matters.
\begin{lemma}[An isolated nonzero coefficient between long zero blocks]\label{lem:bounded-pulse}
Let $a_n\in\Z$ satisfy $|a_n|\le C$. Suppose that for arbitrarily large $L$
there is $N>L$ such that $a_N\ne0$ and
$a_{N+t}=0$ for $0<|t|\le L$. Then $\sum_{n\ge1}a_n2^{-n}$ is irrational.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose that the sum has denominator $q\ge1$. Multiplying it by
$2^j$ and removing its finite integer prefix shows that every scaled
tail $T_j=\sum_{t\ge1}a_{j+t}2^{-t}$ belongs to $q^{-1}\Z$.
Choose a pattern with $C2^{-L}<1/q$. The block on the right gives
\[
 |T_N|\le C\sum_{t>L}2^{-t}=C2^{-L}<1/q.
\]
The only element of $q^{-1}\Z$ in this interval is zero, so $T_N=0$.
The right block has removed the unknown tail exactly. Starting before
the left block now leaves only the nonzero centre, rescaled:
\[
 T_{N-L-1}=a_N2^{-L-1},\qquad
 0<|T_{N-L-1}|\le C2^{-L-1}<1/q,
\]
contradicting $T_{N-L-1}\in q^{-1}\Z$.
\end{proof}
For example, the indicator of the squares satisfies the lemma.
An eventually periodic sequence with infinitely many nonzero terms
does not have isolated coefficients at arbitrarily large distances.
The uniform bound $C$ is essential to this argument.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{res:residueseries}]
We prescribe a prime at the centre and a different divisor at each
neighbour. Fix a unit $s\pmod m$ and an integer $L\ge1$, and choose
distinct primes $q_t\equiv1\pmod m$, all exceeding $L$, for
$0<|t|\le L$. The congruences
\[
 p\equiv s\pmod m,\qquad p\equiv-t\pmod{q_t}\quad(0<|t|\le L)
\]
define a reduced progression, since $s$ is a unit modulo $m$ and
$0<|t|<q_t$. CRT and Dirichlet's theorem therefore allow us to choose
an arbitrarily large prime $p>L+1$ on this progression, with
$m\mid\varphi(p+t)$ at every neighbour and
$\varphi(p)\equiv s-1\pmod m$ at the centre.

For a rational-valued function $f$ on the residue classes, subtract
$f(0)$ and multiply by a common denominator of its values. Since
$\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n}=1$, these operations preserve whether the sum is
rational. If $f(s-1)\ne f(0)$, the resulting bounded integer sequence
has an isolated nonzero coefficient for every $L$, so the lemma
applies.
For the least-residue map, $s=-1$ gives the nonzero centre $m-2$
when $m\ge3$. For $m=2^k$, the possible centres $s-1$ run through
\emph{every} even class. Thus any failure of constancy on those
classes supplies a centre with $f(s-1)\ne f(0)$.
Conversely, constancy makes every term after $n=2$ equal $c$, giving
$3f(1)/4+c/4$.
\end{proof}
The dyadic modulus matters to the classification. Modulo $6$, for
example, prime centres of this form see only $s-1\in\{0,4\}$, not
the even class $2$. The least-residue assertion needs just one
nonzero centre; classification of an arbitrary function needs all
relevant classes.

The first assertion is also an application of Erd\H{o}s's sparse-series
criterion~\cite[Lem.~1, p.~213]{erdos1957}, and of Kaneko, Suzuki and
Tachiya~\cite[Thm.~3]{kst2026}. The residues are bounded and nonnegative,
and the prime construction above makes their support infinite.
The nonzero residues occur on a set of density zero: an integer in that
set has no prime divisor
$p\equiv1\pmod m$. Wong gave the case in which the base equals the
modulus~\cite{wong2015}. The isolated-coefficient argument above also
treats signed values of $f-f(0)$, for which those nonnegative
sparse-series criteria need an additional spacing hypothesis.
The \longrecord{long249-r3-residue-extension}{extension to other bases}
treats every integer $t\ge2$ and proves rational linear
independence of $1$ and $\sum_n(\varphi(n)\bmod m)t^{-dn}$, $d\ge1$.

\appendix
\section{Further consequences for the sections}\label{app:sources}
\papersectiontarget{short249-sources}
Every finite set of dyadic sections lies in a single finite level.
Theorem~\ref{thm:kkernelrank} therefore also determines the full kernel;
``span'' and ``relation'' here still mean finite linear combinations.

\begin{corollary}[Dyadic basis]\label{res:basis}
The family
\[
 \{\ph_{0,0},\ph_{1,0}\}
 \cup\{\ph_{j,r}:j\ge1,\ 0<r<2^j,\ r\text{ odd}\},
 \qquad \ph_{j,r}(n)=\ph(2^jn+r),
\]
is a basis for the rational span of the full dyadic kernel. Every rational
relation is generated by the scalar reductions. The complete level-zero
truncation has dimension one.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Each finite subset of this family is contained in some
$\mathcal B_{2,e}$. Theorem~\ref{thm:kkernelrank} gives independence,
and its reductions give spanning. At level zero the sole section
$\varphi(n)$ is nonzero, since $\varphi(1)=1$.
\end{proof}

The affine argument also permits periodic coefficients by restriction
to their common residue classes.
\begin{corollary}[Periodic coefficients]\label{cor:periodic-freezing}
Let $L_1,\ldots,L_s$ be pairwise nonproportional affine forms with integer
coefficients and positive slopes. If $w_1,\ldots,w_s$ are rational-valued
periodic sequences, then
\[
 \sum_i w_i(n)\ph(L_i(n))=0\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }n
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad w_i(n)=0\quad\text{for every }i,n.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
We choose a common period $Q$ and restrict to $n=r+Qt$. The
coefficients are now the constants $w_i(r)$, and the cross
determinants are $Q(a_i b_j-a_j b_i)\ne0$. By shifting $t$ beyond
the given threshold we can apply affine independence, obtaining
$w_i(r)=0$ for every $i$. We repeat this for each residue $r$;
periodicity then gives the conclusion even at the indices preceding
the threshold.
\end{proof}
Proportional forms are excluded for a reason: the identity
$\varphi(4n+2)=\varphi(2n+1)$ would otherwise contradict the conclusion.
Martin's theorem gives the same corollary on each
progression~\cite[Thm.~1]{martin-phi-inequalities}.

Coons proves nonregularity using the poles of
$\zeta(s-1)/\zeta(s)$~\cite[Cor.~3.1, Thm.~3.2]{coons}.
The ranks above recover it: finite rational kernel dimension would
embed the integral kernel module by evaluations in $\Z^d$, making
it finitely generated; the converse is immediate
(compare~\cite[App.~A]{coons-jsr}).
Allouche, Shallit and Yassawi survey the earlier separation method
\cite[Thm.~3, Ex.~4, Rem.~7]{allouche-shallit-yassawi}.

The generating function $F_\varphi(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}\varphi(n)z^n$
therefore satisfies no $k$-Mahler equation
$\sum_{i=0}^dP_i(z)F_\varphi(z^{k^i})=0$ with $P_i\in\Q[z]$,
$P_0\ne0$. Indeed, $\varphi(n)\le n$ gives logarithmic height at most
$\log n$, and the height theorem of Adamczewski, Bell and Smertnig
would make such a series $k$-regular
\cite[Thm.~1.2(b)]{adamczewski-bell-smertnig2023}.
Bell and Smertnig's multiplicative classification gives the same
conclusion~\cite[Thm.~1.3]{bell-smertnig2026}.
Bell, Bruin and Coons treat related algebraic and $D$-finite series
(those satisfying polynomial-coefficient linear differential equations)
\cite[Thms.~1.5--1.6]{bell-bruin-coons}.
These are statements about the function, not its value at $1/2$.

The section operators $T_i g(n)=g(kn+i)$ satisfy
\[
 T_iF_{j,r}=F_{j+1,k^ji+r},\qquad
 V_{k,e+1}=V_{k,e}+\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}T_iV_{k,e}.
\]
Every residue at level $j+1$ has the form $k^ji+r$, giving the second
identity. A positive retained residue stays retained. For the zero-residue
generators, reduce $T_iF_{0,0}=F_{1,i}$ and $T_iF_{1,0}=F_{2,ki}$ as
before. Each image is a positive integer multiple of a basis element,
but rank growth prevents a finite invariant truncation. Consequently
the growth formula using the joint spectral radius for regular sequences
\cite[Thm.~1, Prop.~4, Cor.~7]{coons-jsr} does not apply.

\section{The binary totient series}\label{sec:carry-rank}
\papersectiontarget{short249-tails}
The bounded-pulse argument in Theorem~\ref{res:residueseries} uses a
tail bound independent of the pulse's position. For $S$, the bound
$0\le\varphi(n)\le n$ ensures convergence, but forcing
$2^L\mid\varphi(N+L)$ with $N+L>1$ requires $2^L\le N+L-1$.
The tail bound $(N+L+2)2^{-L}$ then exceeds $1$.
This is a failure of the estimate, not a lower bound on the tail:
the window lies too far out for this bound to help.
Instead, we test differences of scaled tails by finite sums.

Put $R_N=\sum_{j\ge1}\varphi(N+j)2^{-j}$ and
$\Delta_h(N)=R_{N+h}-R_N$. Subtracting the finite-prefix identities
for $2^{N+h}S$ and $2^NS$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tail-phase}
 \Delta_h(N)\equiv2^N(2^h-1)S\pmod\Z.
\end{equation}
If $S=a/(2^cv)$, with $v$ odd, then $\Delta_h(N)$ is integral for
$N\ge c$ and $h=\varphi(v)$. The tails are then periodic modulo
integers, not necessarily equal. To disprove rationality it therefore
suffices to find a nonintegral difference beyond every threshold for
each positive $h$.

For $h,N,L\in\N$, define the integer
\[
 D_{h,N,L}=\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}
   \bigl(\varphi(N+h+1+j)-\varphi(N+1+j)\bigr)2^{L-1-j},
 \qquad B=N+h+L+2.
\]
Since $0\le R_M\le M+2$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tail-error}
 2^L\Delta_h(N)-D_{h,N,L}=R_{N+h+L}-R_{N+L},\qquad
 |2^L\Delta_h(N)-D_{h,N,L}|\le B.
\end{equation}
Both tails lie in $[0,B]$, so their difference has magnitude at most
$B$, not $2B$. The interval centred at $D_{h,N,L}/2^L$ with radius
$B/2^L$ avoids every integer precisely when
\begin{equation}\label{eq:r3-certificate}
 B<D_{h,N,L}\bmod2^L<2^L-B.
\end{equation}
This proves $\Delta_h(N)\notin\Z$ and, by \eqref{eq:tail-phase},
excludes every reduced denominator dividing $2^N(2^h-1)$.
For example, $D_{1,12,16}=-143140$ has residue $53468$ modulo $2^{16}$,
and $B=31$, so it excludes denominators dividing $2^{12}$.
In ordinary coordinates the same certificate reads
\[
 \Delta_1(12)\in
 \left[\frac{-143171}{65536},\frac{-143109}{65536}\right]
 \subset(-3,-2).
\]

For fixed $h,N$, the test is complete: if
$\delta=\operatorname{dist}(\Delta_h(N),\Z)>0$, then
$2^L\delta>2B$ for all large $L$, since $B$ grows linearly.
Together with \eqref{eq:tail-error}, this gives \eqref{eq:r3-certificate}.
A failed test proves no integrality; its interval may be too wide.
Depth detects a given nonintegral difference, but does not supply one
for each $h$ beyond every threshold.

\subsection{Equivalent residue conditions}\label{sec:frontier}
We write $K(h,N,L)$ for \eqref{eq:r3-certificate}.
\begin{theorem}[Propagation of one nonintegral tail difference]\label{res:fulldepth}
Fix $d\ge1$ and $N\ge0$. If $\Delta_d(N)\notin\Z$, then every sufficiently
late pair $\{t,t+1\}$ contains an $m$ such that $K(md,N,md)$ holds.
Consequently
\[
 \exists t\ge1:\ K(td,N,td)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Delta_d(N)\notin\Z.
\]
Requiring this for every $d\ge1,N\ge0$ is equivalent to $S\notin\Q$.
\end{theorem}
Completeness fixes $h,N$ and varies $L$; here $L=h=td$.
A failed test puts $\Delta_{td}(N)$ within
$2(N+2td+2)2^{-td}$ of $\Z$. This bound tends to zero. The recurrence
$\Delta_{(t+1)d}(N)\equiv2^d\Delta_{td}(N)+\Delta_d(N)\pmod\Z$
would transfer two consecutive errors to the fixed nonintegral
$\Delta_d(N)$. Its positive distance from $\Z$ therefore rules out
consecutive failures for large $t$.
The \longrecord{long249-r3-ray}{companion proof} gives the estimates.
The final assertion still quantifies over every $d,N$, not one pair.

For a hypothetical denominator $2^cv$, a second test uses the
modulus $M=(2^H-1)/v$, where $H$ is a positive multiple of $\varphi(v)$.
Write $B_{H,c}=\sum_{j=0}^{H-1}\varphi(c+1+j)2^{H-1-j}$.
\begin{equivform}[A residue test modulo a divisor of $2^H-1$]\label{res:canonicalmersenne}
The series $S$ is irrational if and only if, for every $c\ge0$ and odd
$v\ge1$, some positive multiple $H$ of $\ph(v)$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:canonical-gap}
 c+H+1<(-B_{H,c})\bmod M<M-(c+H+1).
\end{equation}
\end{equivform}
The identity $B_{H,c}=M(vR_c)-\Delta_H(c)$ puts $B_{H,c}$ within
$c+H+1$ of $M(vR_c)$. If $S=a/(2^cv)$, then $vR_c\in\Z$,
so the residue lies near an endpoint. For irrational $S$, the fixed
number $vR_c$ has positive distance from $\Z$. The distance of $M(vR_c)$ from
$M\Z$ grows exponentially, while the error bound and excluded
margins grow linearly.
The \longrecord{long249-r3-mersenne}{proof and residue recurrence}
give the bounds.
The required residues have not been shown to exist for every choice
of the parameters in either test. A separate
\longrecord{long249-r3-farey}{Farey-interval calculation} at depth $240$
excludes $S=a/q$ for $0<q\le Q_0\approx7.96\times10^{34}$.

\subsection{Comparison sequences}\label{sec:nogo}\label{sec:signed-interpolation-transfer}
Rationality and linear coefficient growth still permit exponential
carry rank. There is an integer sequence $c$ with $0\le c(n)\le n$, unchanged odd totients and
$|c(n)-\varphi(n)|\le2$ at even indices, for which
$\sum c(n)2^{-n}=5/4$. Its carry is the integer sequence
\[
 u_N=4\sum_{j\ge1}c(N+j)2^{-j}
     =5\cdot2^N-4\sum_{n=1}^{N}c(n)2^{N-n}.
\]
Its recurrence is $2u_{N-1}-u_N=4c(N)$ for $N\ge1$.
For $j\ge1$ and odd $0<r<2^j$, this gives
\[
 4\varphi(2^jn+r)=2u_{2^jn+r-1}-u_{2^jn+r}.
\]
Thus the $2^e-1$ independent odd-residue totient sections lie in the
span of the carry sections through level $e$. This explains how the
rank lower bound survives even though the sum is rational.
The \longrecord{long249-r3-comparisons}{construction and its limitations}
explain why it fails the exact prime-dilation laws of $\varphi$.
The same section retains the cofinal LCM-diagonal criterion, its endpoint
sign conditions and the limits of finite integer combinations of shifts.

The \longrecord{long249-r3-interpolation}{signed interpolation
argument} tests whether preserving specified analytic data fixes the
value. For each integer $\beta\ge2$, sparse even-index corrections
realise every value in an interval about $\sum\varphi(n)\beta^{-n}$,
with a prescribed prefix and all odd coefficients fixed. Errors are
bounded by any prescribed positive $f(n)\to\infty$; their support has
upper Banach density zero. On each fixed arithmetic progression the
Dirichlet-series difference is entire. At roots of unity the
generating-function difference extends smoothly radially, with any
prescribed finite collection of radial derivatives zero. This preserves
Dirichlet singularities, not regular parts or zeros; a finite jet is
not the full radial germ. The proof is not formalised in Lean and
estimates no cancellation for the unchanged totient sequence.

Rational approximation imposes a different requirement. The identity
\[
 \Theta_2:=\sum_{d\ge1}\frac{\mu(d)}{(2^d-1)^2}=S-\frac12
\]
was posted by Amiram Eldar, together with its coprimality interpretation,
on 15 March 2026~\cite{eldar2026oeis}, and by Steve Fan on
16 May 2026~\cite{fan2026totient}.
Consider the rational quotients
\[
 Q(e,Y)=\frac{\bigl(\sum_{d\le Y}\mu(d)/(2^d-1)^{e+2}\bigr)^2}
      {\sum_{d\le Y}\mu(d)/(2^d-1)^{2e+2}}.
\]
\begin{theorem}[A lower bound for the rank-one quotients]\label{res:rankonefloor}
For $e\ge1$ and $Y\ge4$, the denominator of $Q(e,Y)$ is positive, and the
unique minimiser is $(e,Y)=(1,5)$. Every admissible quotient and every
nonempty finite positive weighted average of such quotients satisfies
\[
 Q-\Theta_2>\frac{21}{320}.
\]
The uniform bound $Q-\Theta_2>1/15$ is false already at $(1,5)$.
\end{theorem}
The \longrecord{long249-r3-rankone}{proof} first makes the denominator
uniformly positive. A geometric bound handles all $e\ge2$; at $e=1$,
seven-term prefixes leave only $Y=4,5,6$ to compare directly.
The averaging assertion concerns averages of the quotients themselves.
It leaves open signed combinations, quotients formed after combining
the sums, and higher-rank kernels. For a denominator-clearing
irrationality argument, a sufficient target is
$0<q_j|\Theta_2-p_j/q_j|\to0$, with $p_j/q_j$ in lowest terms.
Indeed, if $\Theta_2=a/b$, any nonzero difference satisfies
$q_j|a/b-p_j/q_j|=|a q_j-bp_j|/b\ge1/b$.
Convergence alone gives no such contradiction.

\section{An exponential-sum question}\label{sec:open}
\papersectiontarget{short249-first-harmonic}
To prove irrationality, it suffices to show that for every $h\ge1$
and every $X_0$, some integers $X\ge\max(X_0,1)$ and $L\ge h$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:r3-harmonic}
 16(2X+h+L+2)\le2^L,\qquad
 \operatorname{Re}\sum_{N=X}^{2X-1}
       \exp(2\pi iD_{h,N,L}/2^L)\le\frac9{10}X.
\end{equation}
The phases cannot all cluster near $1$. If every residue failed
\eqref{eq:r3-certificate}, each $D_{h,N,L}/2^L$ would be within
$1/16$ of an integer. Each exponential would then have real part at least
$\cos(\pi/8)>9/10$. Thus some $N$ satisfies
\eqref{eq:r3-certificate}. For a hypothetical rational value, choosing
its period and a sufficiently late block contradicts
\eqref{eq:tail-phase}.

To separate counting from cancellation, single out one totient in
each window. Fix $h,s\ge1$,
$L\ge s+h$, $X\ge1$ and $0<\eta<1$, and put
$t=L-s+1$ and $E_N=\exp(2\pi iD_{h,N,L}/2^L)$.
For $X\le N<2X$, let $p_N$ be the largest prime factor of $N+t$ and
$m_N=(N+t)/p_N$. Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal A&=\{N\in[X,2X):m_N\le\lfloor\sqrt X/2\rfloor,
                      \ p_N>2\lfloor\sqrt X\rfloor\},\\
 \mathcal G&=\{N\in\mathcal A:\varphi(m_N)\ge\eta m_N\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All indices are integers. On $\mathcal A$, $p_N>m_N$, hence
$\varphi(N+t)=\varphi(m_N)(p_N-1)$. Since $h<t\le L$, this term
occurs in both tails, with net coefficient
$2^{-(t-h)}-2^{-t}=(2^h-1)/2^t$. Write
\[
 z_N=\exp\!\left(\frac{2\pi i(2^h-1)\varphi(m_N)(p_N-1)}{2^t}\right),
 \qquad w_N=E_N/z_N,
\]
and let $\bar z_m$ be the average over the indices in $\mathcal A$
with cofactor $m$, or zero for an empty set.
For fixed $m$, the exponent of $z_N$ is affine in $p_N$;
$w_N$ contains the other totients.

Consider the four bounds
\begin{equation}\label{eq:r3-four-bounds}
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Re}\sum_{N\in\mathcal G}w_N(z_N-\bar z_{m_N})
       &\le\tfrac{14}{25}X,\\
 \left|\sum_{N\in\mathcal G}w_N\bar z_{m_N}\right|
       &\le\tfrac1{100}X,\\
 \left|\sum_{N\in\mathcal A\smallsetminus\mathcal G}E_N\right|
       &\le\tfrac1{100}X,\\
 \left|\sum_{\substack{X\le N<2X\\N\notin\mathcal A}}E_N\right|
       &\le\tfrac8{25}X.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
These are an exact partition: outside $\mathcal G$ use the last two
sums; on $\mathcal G$ write
$w_Nz_N=w_N(z_N-\bar z_{m_N})+w_N\bar z_{m_N}$.
The bounds add to $(14/25+1/100+1/100+8/25)X=9X/10$.

The last three bounds are available at a common depth. Take the least
$L\ge s+h$ satisfying the size inequality in \eqref{eq:r3-harmonic}.
The \longrecord{long249-r3-counts}{smooth-number and small-cofactor estimates}
give the last two bounds for all large $X$ when
$0<\eta<1/(300\log4)$. The elementary excluded-cofactor estimate is
$(3\eta\log4+o(1))X$; it needs no prime number theorem.
With the prime number theorem as input, the
\longrecord{long249-group-mean}{group-mean estimate} gives the second
bound for $s=26$, $\eta=1/1000$ at this depth and all large $X$.
The first bound remains open.

Small group means control the second sum by the triangle inequality
because $|w_N|=1$. They do not control the first: subtracting
$\bar z_m$ cancels an \emph{unweighted} group sum, not one with
varying $w_N$. No independence is assumed.
For example, $z=(1,-1)$ has mean zero, but the weights
$w=(1,-1)$ make $\sum w_N(z_N-\bar z)=2$.
This illustrates the distinction, not the behaviour of the totient phases.
A real-part bound does not control the imaginary part or give the
$21X/25$ norm bound.

\begin{problem}[Four estimates for the first-harmonic sum]
\label{prob:firstharmonic}
For each $h\ge1$, do there exist $s\ge1$ and $0<\eta<1$ such that, for every
$X_0$, there are $X,L$ with
\[
 \max(X_0,1)\le X,\qquad h\le L-s,\qquad
 16(2X+h+L+2)\le2^L,
\]
for which those four bounds hold?
\end{problem}

Fix $s,\eta$ after $h$ but before $X_0$; all four estimates must hold
on the same block. At $s=26$, $\eta=1/1000$ and the least admissible
$L$, it suffices to prove the first bound for arbitrarily large $X$:
the other three hold eventually on those same blocks.

A weaker sufficient condition needs no group-mean input.
Since $|\mathcal G|>67X/100$ for large $X$, the open bound
$\operatorname{Re}\sum_{N\in\mathcal G}E_N\le603X/1000$
would put the average on $\mathcal G$ below $9/10$:
$603/1000=(9/10)(67/100)$. Some good index would pass the test.
This requires an average on $\mathcal G$ for each $h$ on arbitrarily
large blocks, not a bound on the full block.
The \longrecord{long249-r3-interpolation}{ordinary comparison argument}
gives larger first harmonics at all sufficiently large admissible scales,
distinguishing its rational sequences from the cancellation required of
$\varphi$.

Balasubramanian, Giri and Srivastav give correlation estimates applicable
to $\varphi(n)/n$, uniformly for $|h|\le x/2$~\cite[Thm.~2.2]{bgs2016}.
Their correlation is a product of two normalised totient values.
Here the modulus grows with $L$, and $w_N$ is an exponential of the
other, overlapping totient contributions. The cited shift uniformity
does not supply this weighted exponential estimate.

\section*{Verification and reproducibility}
\evidenceparagraph{\evidencerecordurl}
The \longrecord{long249-r3-declarations}{declaration guide} links the

appear in Appendix~A of the companion paper. The displayed arguments,
including signed interpolation, require ordinary mathematical review;
the recorded Lean and Comparator checks cover their specified

excerpts.text:
Rationality of $S=\sum_{n\ge1}\varphi(n)2^{-n}$ forces a positive
shift for which every sufficiently late difference of scaled tails
is an integer. We develop finite residue tests for a failure of this
integrality and prove their completeness and propagation laws.
The tests yield a finite denominator exclusion, but their required
supply at arbitrarily large indices remains unproved. Rational
comparison sequences explain why coefficient rank, finite data and
specified analytic properties do not supply it. A first-harmonic
route isolates the remaining weighted cancellation estimate; its
group-mean bound is recorded with a prime-number-theorem input.
The irrationality of $S$ remains open.

\section*{Organisation}
The argument starts from $2^NS=\Phi_N+R_N$, with $\Phi_N\in\Z$.
A rational $S$ gives a shift $h>0$ for which $R_{N+h}-R_N\in\Z$
for every sufficiently large $N$. Three questions organise the record.

\emph{What finite calculation can refute that integrality?}
The residue test in Definition~\ref{defn:sep} encloses the tail
difference in an explicit error interval. Section~\ref{sec:series}
gives the identities and the independent Farey-window exclusion.
Appendix~\ref{app:r3-complements} supplies the complete propagation,
Mersenne-residue and rank-one arguments cited in the short paper.

\emph{Which information is insufficient to supply such calculations?}
The \shortpaper{short249-basis}{short paper} determines all finite-level
totient relations, with a basis of $k^e+1$ sections in every base
$k\ge2$. Its \shortpaper{short249-base-six}{integral relation proof}
recovers the coefficients of every relation. Those are statements
about sequences, not their weighted infinite sums.
Section~\ref{sec:mahler-defect} explains the distinction through
carry rank; Section~\ref{sub:generic-carry-rank} constructs a rational
$5/4$ series retaining the odd totients. Section~\ref{sec:wall}
gives other comparisons, each limited to its stated preserved properties.

\emph{What additional estimate would suffice?}
Section~\ref{sec:survivors} gives the quantified conditions.
Section~\ref{sub:pivot} separates the weighted exponential-sum estimate
from the counting and group-mean bounds, corresponding to the
\shortpaper{short249-first-harmonic}{four-estimate problem} in the
short paper. A second sufficient condition estimates only the average
over good indices and needs no group-mean input.
Appendix~\ref{app:r3-declarations} records the formal declarations;
an implication proved there does not establish its remaining hypothesis.

\setcounter{tocdepth}{1}
\clearpage
\tableofcontents
\clearpage
% ; - part a249_front ; -

\subsection{Counterexamples and limitations}

A residue or coefficient condition may hold for a rational comparison
series as well as for $S$. Each example below records the information
it preserves and the deduction it disproves. The irrationality of $S$
remains open, and an argument using further totient identities is
unaffected by a comparison that does not preserve them.


\begin{obs}[The sign of the actual endpoint representative]\label{prop:SGN-02}
Assume $a\ge8$, $H=H_{2^a}$ and
$J+K+a+6<2\cdot2^a$, as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:SGN-01}. If
$d=R_{2H+J}-R_{H+J}$ is an integer, define
\[
 c_0=d,\qquad
 c_{j+1}=2c_j-\bigl(\varphi(2H+J+j+1)-\varphi(H+J+j+1)\bigr).
\]
The tail recurrence gives
$c_K=R_{2H+J+K}-R_{H+J+K}>0$. Its negative is an integer
representative satisfying
\[
 |{-c_K}|\le2H+J+K+2,\qquad
 -c_K\equiv D(H,H+J,K)\pmod{2^K}.
\]
Thus the representative corresponding to the actual tail is negative.
The stated size bound allows it to remain in the endpoint interval,
so its sign alone does not contradict integrality. Other integers in
that interval with the same residue need not represent the actual tail.
Proposition~\ref{prop:SGN-03} gives the further residue separation
that would exclude this case.
\lean{actualLcm_trueEndpointSurvivor_neg}{TotientActualLcmOrbitSign.lean:172}
\end{obs}

\begin{obs}[The complete divisibility pattern is impossible]\label{prop:TE-01-killer}
Let $a\ge8$, $H=H_{2^a}$ and $J,K,m\in\mathbb N$. Assume
\[
 m\le K,\qquad J+K+a+6<2\cdot2^a,\qquad
 2H+J+K+2<2^m.
\]
The simultaneous divisibilities
\[
 2^{r+1}\mid\delta_{2^a}(J+K-m+r+1)\qquad(0\le r<m)
\]
cannot hold. The terminal difference would be positive by
Proposition~\ref{prop:AR-05-inv}, smaller than $2^m$, and divisible by
$2^m$, a contradiction. The obstruction applies to this complete
pattern under the stated size bounds. Omitting its last divisibility
condition leads to the necessary restrictions in
Proposition~\ref{prop:TE-02-inv}; the residue inequality in
Proposition~\ref{prop:TE-04} is another sufficient condition. Neither
statement here supplies such witnesses at arbitrarily large scales.
\lean{not_actualLcmTerminalDyadicStaircase_of_room}{TotientActualLcmTopEdgeStaircase.lean:251}
\end{obs}

\begin{obs}[An exact valuation in a dyadically scaled family]\label{prop:FR-03-kill}
For every integer $n\ge0$, take $H=2^{n+2}$ and $j=3\cdot2^{n+1}$.
Then
\[
 \varphi(3H+j)-2\varphi(2H+j)+\varphi(H+j)=-2^{n+1}.
\]
Indeed, the three arguments are $9\cdot2^{n+1}$,
$7\cdot2^{n+1}$ and $5\cdot2^{n+1}$. Their totients are respectively
$6\cdot2^n$, $6\cdot2^n$ and $4\cdot2^n$, which give the identity.
Thus the difference has $2$-adic valuation exactly $n+1$.
This example limits a valuation bound for arbitrary even heights and
scaled odd offsets. Here $j>H$, whereas the offset in
Proposition~\ref{prop:FR-02-inv} is at most $2^{a/2}$ and the height is
$H(2^a)$. The example therefore does not exclude additional divisibility
on that LCM family.
\lean{fixedRankSecondDifference_dyadic_fixture_exact}{TotientFixedRankLcmAsymptotic.lean:462}
\end{obs}

\begin{obs}[A rational sequence with matching parity]\label{prop:CM-01}

Start with the coefficient sequence $0,1,1,2,4,4,4,\ldots$, indexed
from $0$. For each $m=2^{k+3}$, $k\ge0$, replace the pair at positions
$m,m+1$ from $(4,4)$ to $(6,0)$, leaving all other coefficients unchanged.
These pairs are disjoint. Each replacement preserves the binary sum because
\[
 2\cdot2^{-m}-4\cdot2^{-(m+1)}=0.
\]
The resulting sequence has the same sum $3/2$ and the same parity at
every index as $\varphi$. It is not eventually periodic, since the gaps
between its occurrences of $6$ tend to infinity. This construction uses
the particular initial parity pattern and the binary weights; it does
not establish an analogous result for arbitrary prescribed parities or
other summand weights.
\lean{parityCoboundaryWeight}{TotientParityCoboundaryCountermodel.lean:59}
\end{obs}

\begin{obs}[What the parity example disproves]\label{prop:CM-02}
The sequence $c$ in Observation~\ref{prop:CM-01} satisfies
\[
 0\le c(n)\le\min(n,6),\qquad
 c(n)\equiv\varphi(n)\pmod2,\qquad
 \sum_{n\ge0}c(n)2^{-n}=\frac32,
\]
and is not eventually periodic. More precisely, for every
$N,G,K\in\mathbb N$, it has $K$ of the displayed $(6,0)$ pairs
starting beyond $N$, with successive starting positions separated
by more than $G$. Choose sufficiently late powers of two in the
construction to obtain these pairs.
Hence the growth bound, the exact parity pattern, nonperiodicity and
these arbitrarily separated occurrences are compatible with a rational
sum. They cannot by themselves prove irrationality. The construction
does not preserve the complete totient sequence or its
multiplicativity, and does not specify which additional arithmetic
hypothesis would suffice.
\lean{exists_totientParity_arbitrarilyManySeparatedCarry_rational_countermodel}{TotientParityCoboundaryCountermodel.lean:637}
\end{obs}

\begin{obs}[A Mersenne factor does not force tail-difference divisibility]\label{prop:CP-03-kill}
For the completely multiplicative sequence $c(n)=n$, the scaled tail is
\[
 T_N=\sum_{j\ge1}(N+j)2^{-j}=N+2,
 \qquad T_{N+K}-T_N=K.
\]
If $q>K>0$ and $q\mid2^K-1$, then every such tail difference is
integral but is not divisible by $q$. For example, take $K=3$ and
$q=7$; the multiplicative order of $2$ modulo $7$ is $3$.
Thus even this prime divisor of the homogeneous recurrence multiplier
does not force divisibility of the inhomogeneous tail difference.
An application to the totient sequence needs a further relation between
the prime and the coefficient residues or the tail's size. This
example supplies no general obstruction for Problem~\#257 merely
because that problem also involves Mersenne denominators. Compare the
specific totient construction in Proposition~\ref{prop:CP-05-inv}.
\lean{idCoeff_mersenneModulus_does_not_annihilate_tailShift}{TotientTailCarryPeriod.lean:342}
\end{obs}

\begin{obs}[A lower bound for the stated rec

\subsection{Scope of the index}

The index compares particular quantified hypotheses and the results
that use them. An unsuccessful implication between two entries
therefore says nothing by itself about every argument using the same
method.

Each entry states its quantifiers in full. A cofinal assertion, with a
quantifier of the form $\forall a_0\ \exists a\ge a_0$, may itself be
proved or may remain an unproved hypothesis; the text of each entry says
which. A cofinal assertion about a different quantity, or with a
different order of quantifiers, need not supply the irrationality
condition.

The quantified residue condition for \#249, stated in Definition~\ref{defn:sep} and proved sufficient
(\lean{irrational_totient_series_of_certificate_supply}{TotientTailPeriodKiller.lean:394}), is the
following statement:
\[
  \forall h \ge 1,\ \forall N_0,\ \exists N \ge N_0,\ \exists L,\ \mathcal{C}\ h\ N\ L .
\]
The following catalogue compares fourteen proposed approaches to this
condition. It starts with the exponential-sum estimate, then gives thirteen
further approaches with their individual hypotheses and source references.

excerpts.section: Positivity and the remaining residue inequality
excerpts.text:
\subsubsection{Positivity and the remaining residue inequality}

\begin{defn}
The \emph{actual LCM tail orbit} at exponent $a$ is
$\Omega_a = R_{2H}-R_H$, where $H = {H}(2^a)$
(\lean{actualLcmTailOrbit_pos}{TotientActualLcmOrbitSign.lean:144}).
\end{defn}

\begin{thm}\label{thm:positivity-remaining-residue-inequality}
For every $a\ge 8$ and every $J$ with $J+(a{+}6) < 2\cdot 2^a$,
\[
  0 \;<\; {R}(2H{+}J) - {R}(H{+}J), \qquad H={H}(2^a).
\]
Hence $0 < \Omega_a$ for every $a\ge 8$. The proof is genuinely uniform in
$a$: it rests on two facts proved for all $a\ge 8$ and $0<j<2^{a+1}$, namely $\delta_{2^a}(j)>0$ and $H<8\cdot 2^a\,\delta_{2^a}(j)$, by a two-case structural split (divisor letter
vs.\ foreign prime power), with absolute constants $4,8,32$ and no lookup table.
\end{thm}

\begin{rem}[Which endpoint interval must be excluded]
Under the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:SGN-03}, integrality would
force the residue to be $2^K-e$, where
$e=R_{2H+J+K}-R_{H+J+K}$ is a positive integer smaller than
$2H+J+K+2$. Thus the residue lies near the upper endpoint, not near zero
in its least nonnegative representation. The representative $-e$ is
negative; the carry $e$ is positive.

The one-sided test below excludes precisely that upper interval. This
uses the bound $J+K+(a+6)<2\cdot2^a$, as well as the modulus bound.
It does not follow from positivity that the residue already satisfies
half of a nonintegrality certificate without those assumptions.
\end{rem}

\runninghead{Erd\H{o}s \#251: sparse perturbations and exact criteria}
\title{Sparse Congruence-Preserving Perturbations\\of Dyadic Series}
\subtitle{What gap statistics can tell us about Erd\H{o}s Problem~\#251}
\author{Will Cook}
\date{September 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle
\noteprovenance

\begin{abstract}
We perturb convergent dyadic series with nonnegative integer coefficients
to attain both rational and irrational sums while preserving eventual
congruences and asymptotic block statistics.  Nonnegative corrections on
one set of upper Banach density zero attain a nondegenerate interval above
the original sum.  They eventually respect any prescribed bound tending
to infinity and preserve coefficient and partial-sum residues for every
fixed modulus, with target-independent cutoffs.  We vary adjacent correction pairs
with fixed ordinary totals; growing digit ranges let later weighted
choices fill the gaps between present choices.  Applied to prime gaps with
correction bound $\log(n+3)$, this preserves cumulative growth $n\log n$
and gives vanishing total variation error for blocks of length
$o(\log\log X)$ sampled on $[X,2X)$.  Cumulative positions need not be
prime; irrationality of the actual prime series remains open.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:problem}
Let $p_0=2,p_1=3,\ldots$ be the primes and put $g_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$.
Erd\H{o}s asked whether
\[
 \Pi=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{p_n}{2^{n+1}}
\]
is irrational \cite[p.~94]{erdos1958}\cite[p.~62]{erdosgraham1980}
\cite[p.~103]{erdos1988}.  Summation by parts gives
$\Pi=2+\sum_{n\ge0}g_n2^{-(n+1)}$, with convergence justified in
Section~\ref{sec:parts}.  We study which properties of the gaps survive
when the latter sum is changed to a prescribed value.

The support and every modulus cutoff are fixed before the target is
chosen.  The interval contains rational and irrational sums with the
same eventual coefficient and partial-sum residues.  A block changes
only when it meets the support, whereas every correction enters the
dyadic sum.  With polylogarithmic corrections, empirical block laws
agree asymptotically at lengths $o(\log\log X)$; for prime gaps,
cumulative growth remains $n\log n$.  The comparison positions need
not be consecutive primes.

We use a standard interval-covering argument for series with finite choices.
Fridy's generalised-base lemma \cite[p.~194]{fridy1966} treats prescribed
digit bounds and nonincreasing weights.  Crmari\'{c} and Kova\v{c}
\cite[Lemma~4]{crmarickovac2025} give the finite-choice form used here,
and Kova\v{c} and Tao \cite[Lemma~5.1]{kovactao2024} use analogous
intervals of reciprocal choices.  We must arrange these choices on a sparse set while preserving cumulative
congruences.  To do so, we redistribute a fixed correction between two adjacent
indices.  The simplest useful calculation is
\[
 \begin{array}{c|rrrr}
 (e_n,e_{n+1}) &(0,6)&(2,4)&(4,2)&(6,0)\\
 e_n+e_{n+1} &6&6&6&6\\
 2^{n+2}\bigl(e_n2^{-n-1}+e_{n+1}2^{-n-2}\bigr)&6&8&10&12.
 \end{array}
\]
Moving $2$ from the later index to the earlier one changes the weighted
sum while leaving the ordinary sum fixed.  If the cumulative correction
before the pair is odd, an additional $1$ at $n-1$ clears its residue
modulo $2$.  Since the four pairs have the same sum, the choice of pair leaves every
later cumulative residue unchanged.  We repeat this operation with
nested moduli and increasingly separated pairs.  The larger separations
make the weighted contributions smaller, so we enlarge the range of each
pair until the later contributions fill the gaps between consecutive
present choices.

Throughout, $\N=\{0,1,\ldots\}$, intervals of indices contain integers,
and $\log$ is natural unless a base is displayed.  A set $S\subseteq\N$
has \emph{upper Banach density zero} if
\[
 \lim_{H\to\infty}\sup_{u\in\N}\frac{|S\cap[u,u+H)|}{H}=0.
\]
For integers $X,m\ge1$, let $\mu_{a,X,m}$ denote the distribution of
$(a_n,\ldots,a_{n+m-1})$ when $n$ is uniform on $[X,2X)$.  The entries
are not rescaled: we sample starting indices, not distinct block values.  We use
$d_{\rm TV}(\mu,\nu)=\sup_B|\mu(B)-\nu(B)|$, with the supremum over all sets of blocks.

\begin{proposition}[sparse changes preserving congruences]\label{res:sparserationalisation}
Let $a:\N\to\N$ satisfy $A=\sum_{n\ge0}a_n2^{-(n+1)}<\infty$,
let $K\in\N$, and let $f:\N\to\R$ tend to $+\infty$.
There exist a set $S\subseteq[K,\infty)$ of upper Banach density zero
and a nondegenerate interval $I\subset(A,\infty)$ such that, for every
$r\in I$, there is an integer correction $e:\N\to\N$ satisfying
\[
 \operatorname{supp}e\subseteq S,\qquad e_n\le f(n)\ \text{eventually},
 \qquad \sum_{n\ge0}(a_n+e_n)2^{-(n+1)}=r.
\]
For each integer $q\ge1$ there is a cutoff $N_q$, independent of $r$,
such that $q\mid e_n$ and $q\mid\sum_{i<n}e_i$ for all $n\ge N_q$.
For every $\varepsilon>0$, the choice $f(n)=(\log(n+3))^\varepsilon$
can be made with
\[
 |S\cap[X,2X)|=O_\varepsilon\!\left(\frac{X}{\log\log X}\right),
 \qquad
 d_{\rm TV}(\mu_{a,X,m},\mu_{a+e,X,m})
 \le\frac{m|S\cap[X,2X+m)|}{X}.
\]
In particular the distance tends to zero for every integer-valued
$m=m(X)\ge1$ with $m(X)=o(\log\log X)$, uniformly over target values.
\end{proposition}

The cutoff may depend on $q$, but $S$ and all cutoffs are fixed before
$r$.  Only $e$ varies with the target, and its support may occupy just
part of $S$.  Infinitely many changes are essential: finitely many
integer dyadic corrections add a rational number.  The allowance may
grow as slowly as $\log\log(n+3)$, but it cannot be bounded.  A modulus
exceeding the bound would force $e$ eventually to vanish; its constant
cumulative sum would then be divisible by every positive integer.
Nonnegativity forces $e=0$.  Polynomially growing coefficients satisfy
the convergence hypothesis; $a_n=2^n$ does not.

Section~\ref{sec:construction} proves the construction and
Section~\ref{sec:prime-application} transfers the stated prime-gap properties.
For the actual primes, integral tail shifts characterise rationality.
Two consecutive small differences with unequal gaps give a sufficient
condition for irrationality.  Finite enclosures certify individual
witnesses without supplying arbitrarily late ones.  The
\href{erdos251-prime-gap-reasoning-surface.pdf\#context}{companion's literature discussion}
contains the further comparisons, including finite subsums and other
dyadic coefficient sequences.

\section{Proof of Proposition~\ref{res:sparserationalisation}}\label{sec:construction}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Fixed totals.}
Use $n_j-1$ to cancel a cumulative residue and $n_j,n_j+1$ for a
pair with fixed ordinary sum.  Varying the pair changes its weighted
contribution without altering any later residue to be cancelled.
Choose an initial index $n_{-1}\ge K$ and centres with
$s_j=n_j-n_{j-1}\ge4$, so the triples do not overlap.  Let
$M_j$ be positive integers with $M_j\mid M_{j+1}$, and let $D_j$
bound the digit at stage $j$.  The spacing, moduli and digit bounds
will be chosen below.

Let $C_j$ record the ordinary correction before the $j$th triple.
Starting from $C_0=0$, prescribe
\[
 c_j=(-C_j)\bmod M_j\quad(0\le c_j<M_j),\qquad
 C_{j+1}=C_j+c_j+M_jD_j.
\]
For integers $0\le d_j\le D_j$, set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:correction-triple}
 e_{n_j-1}=c_j,\qquad e_{n_j}=M_jd_j,\qquad
 e_{n_j+1}=M_j(D_j-d_j),
\end{equation}
and put $e_n=0$ elsewhere.  The two sums of a triple are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{r=n_j-1}^{n_j+1}e_r
    &=c_j+M_jD_j,\\
 \sum_{r=n_j-1}^{n_j+1}e_r2^{-r-1}
    &=c_j2^{-n_j}+M_jD_j2^{-n_j-2}+d_jM_j2^{-n_j-2}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The ordinary total contains no $d_j$, so the recurrence fixes every
$c_j$ in advance.  In the weighted total only the last term varies:
transferring $M_j$ from $n_j+1$ to $n_j$ adds
\[
 w_j=M_j2^{-n_j-2}.
\]

After $c_j$ has been inserted, the cumulative correction is divisible
by $M_j$; the two entries of the pair preserve this divisibility.
Fix $q\mid M_J$.  At index $n_J$ both the coefficient correction and
the cumulative correction are divisible by $q$.  At every later
triple, $q$ divides $C_j$ and $M_j$, so it also divides $c_j$ and
both pair entries.  The intervening corrections are zero.  Hence
\[
 q\mid e_n,\qquad q\mid\sum_{i<n}e_i\qquad(n\ge n_J).
\]
The entry $c_J$ need not be divisible by $q$, which is why it is placed at
$n_J-1$, before the cutoff.  The index $n_J$ depends on $q$ and the chosen
moduli, but not on the digits or the value to be attained.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{Spacing and size.}
The choices at stage $j$ are $0,w_j,\ldots,D_jw_j$.
The covering argument will work if the later ranges total at least
$w_j$.  Taking $D_i=2^{s_i}-1$ compensates for separation by making
each later range a scaled dyadic difference:
\[
 D_iw_i=(2^{n_i-n_{i-1}}-1)M_i2^{-n_i-2}
       =M_i\bigl(2^{-n_{i-1}-2}-2^{-n_i-2}\bigr).
\]
Because $M_i\ge M_j$ for $i>j$, replacing every later modulus by $M_j$
gives the finite estimate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-overlap}
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{i=j+1}^{J}D_iw_i
 &\ge M_j\sum_{i=j+1}^{J}
       \bigl(2^{-n_{i-1}-2}-2^{-n_i-2}\bigr)\\
 &=w_j-M_j2^{-n_J-2}\qquad(J>j).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
No monotonicity of the weights is needed.  Each entry of
\eqref{eq:correction-triple} is at most $M_j2^{s_j}$, so the size cost of
separating the stages is exponential.  We must fit this product below
the allowance at all three indices, while $s_j\to\infty$ and every
fixed positive integer eventually divides $M_j$.

To allow a nonmonotone bound $f$, put
\[
 h(n)=\inf_{m\ge n}\min(f(m),m).
\]
This nondecreasing lower envelope tends to infinity even when $f$
oscillates.  A bound at $n_{j-1}$ therefore controls all three later
coordinates; the cap by $m$ ensures $e_n\le n$ and hence summability
for every digit choice.
Enlarge $n_{-1}\ge K$ until $h(n_{-1})\ge32$, and set
\[
 k_j=\max\{k\ge2:k!2^{k+2}\le h(n_{j-1})\},\qquad
 M_j=k_j!,\qquad s_j=k_j+2,\qquad n_j=n_{j-1}+s_j.
\]
The maximum exists: $k=2$ is admissible because $2!2^4=32$, and
$k!2^{k+2}\to\infty$.  Since $n_j\to\infty$ and $h$ is nondecreasing
and divergent, $k_j$ is nondecreasing and tends to infinity.  Thus
$M_j\mid M_{j+1}$, every fixed $q$ eventually divides $M_j=k_j!$,
and $s_j=k_j+2\to\infty$.
At every coordinate $n$ of the $j$th triple, this schedule also gives
\[
 0\le e_n\le M_j2^{s_j}\le h(n_{j-1})\le\min(f(n),n).
\]
Let $S=\bigcup_{j\ge0}\{n_j-1,n_j,n_j+1\}$.  For $R\ge4$, all
sufficiently late centres are at least $R$ apart.  Every interval of
length $H$ contains at most $3(H/R+2)$ points from those triples;
the earlier triples add a fixed number, independent of the interval's
position.  Divide by $H$, take the supremum over positions, then let
$H\to\infty$.  The limiting upper bound is $3/R$; letting $R\to\infty$
proves upper Banach density zero.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{Attaining the interval.}
The support and congruence requirements are now settled independently
of the target.  Only the digits remain to be chosen.  Define
\[
 \beta=\sum_{j\ge0}\bigl(c_j2^{-n_j}+D_jw_j\bigr),\qquad
 F_j=\sum_{i\ge j}D_iw_i.
\]
Even zero digits contribute $\beta>0$; $F_j$ is the maximum variable
contribution from stage $j$ onwards.  The size bound makes both finite,
with $F_0>0$ and $F_j\to0$.  The total correction is
\[
 \sum_ne_n2^{-n-1}=\beta+\sum_jd_jw_j.
\]
Taking $J\to\infty$ in \eqref{eq:finite-overlap} now gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:overlap}
 F_{j+1}\ge M_j2^{-n_j-2}=w_j.
\end{equation}
These bounds do not yet prove that every point of $[0,F_j]$ is
attained.  A digit $d$ leaves a remainder in $[0,F_{j+1}]$ precisely
for current remainders in
\[
 [dw_j,dw_j+F_{j+1}],\qquad d=0,\ldots,D_j.
\]
These intervals meet or overlap by \eqref{eq:overlap}, and their union
is $[0,F_j]$ because $F_j=D_jw_j+F_{j+1}$.  Figure~\ref{fig:correction-and-overlap}
shows the two calculations.
