\section{Reciprocal-summable supports}\label{sec:reciprocal-support}
Erd\H{o}s stated the following extension of his pairwise-coprime theorem
\cite[p.~222]{erdos1968}. It follows from
Theorem~\ref{res:weighted-support}, since $h/(2^h-1)\le1$, but the
direct argument explains why reciprocal summability makes the averaging
simpler.

\begin{theorem}[reciprocal-summable supports]\label{res:reciprocal-support}
Let $A\subseteq\Npos$ be infinite.  If
\[
  \sum_{a\in A}\frac1a<\infty,
\]
then \(X_A(b)\) is irrational for every integer \(b\ge2\).
\end{theorem}

Erd\H{o}s also discussed weaker conditions \cite[pp.~222, 226]{erdos1968}.
We do not identify our weighted hypothesis with the conditions he suggested.

Reciprocal summability permits two successive limits: first the
observation length grows with the modulus fixed, then the modulus
grows until each fixed exponent divides it. The two interchanges use
different summable bounds; neither requires a period for the infinite
support.

Fix the integer base $b\ge2$ and put
\[
 w_{b,d}(N)=\frac{b^{N\bmod d}}{b^d-1},\qquad
 T_N^{(b)}=\sum_{d\in A}w_{b,d}(N).
\]
Then $T_N^{(b)}-T_0^{(b)}=\Delta_{b,A}(N)$.
For a fixed positive integer $Q$, the orbit of $Q$ modulo $d$ consists of
$d/g$ residues, where $g=(Q,d)$.  Summing the geometric progression gives
\begin{equation}
 M_{Q,b}(d):=\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac1X\sum_{m=1}^Xw_{b,d}(Qm)
 =\frac{g}{d(b^g-1)}\le\frac1d.
 \label{eq:gcd-orbit-mean}
\end{equation}
The example $b=2$, $Q=4$, $d=6$ in
Section~\ref{sec:eight-return-extensions} has mean $1/9$ for $w_{2,6}$,
but $2/21$ for its displacement. When $d\mid Q$,
$w_{b,d}(Qm)=w_{b,d}(0)$ and the displacement vanishes.

To interchange the sum over exponents and this limit, we use a bound
summable in $d$ for the fixed modulus $Q$.  Counting positive multiples of $d$ gives
\begin{align*}
 \frac1X\sum_{m=1}^Xw_{b,d}(Qm)
 &=\sum_{r\ge1}b^{-r}
       \frac{\#\{1\le m\le X:d\mid Qm+r\}}X\\
 &\le\sum_{r\ge1}b^{-r}\frac{Q+r}{d}
 =\frac{Q/(b-1)+b/(b-1)^2}{d}\le\frac{Q+2}{d}.
\end{align*}
Indeed, the counted multiples are distinct and at most $QX+r$.
For this fixed $Q$, the majorant $(Q+2)/d$ is summable over $A$.
Dominated convergence therefore takes the observation-length limit inside
the sum over $d$, giving the Ces\`aro mean
$\sum_{d\in A}M_{Q,b}(d)$.  This majorant is not uniform in growing $Q$.

Next let $Q_t=\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,t)$.
For each fixed $d$, eventually $d\mid Q_t$ and
$M_{Q_t,b}(d)=(b^d-1)^{-1}$.  A second dominated-convergence argument,
using $M_{Q_t,b}(d)\le1/d$, yields
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{d\in A}M_{Q_t,b}(d)\longrightarrow X_A(b).
 \label{eq:lcm-prefix-orbit-limit}
\end{equation}
The limiting displacement means therefore tend to zero. Choose $t$,
then a sufficiently long finite average, then a term no larger than that
average. The resulting arbitrarily small positive displacements contradict
the rationality bound $1/q$ in~\eqref{eq:intro-displacement}. This proves
Theorem~\ref{res:reciprocal-support} at every integer base.

Powerful integers (all prime exponents at least two) have the form
$u^2v^3$, so their reciprocal sum is at most $\zeta(2)\zeta(3)$.
The theorem therefore applies to every infinite subset. For full
perfect-power supports, compare Duverney--Tachiya
\cite[Corollary~1.2, p.~4]{duverneytachiya} and Luca--Tachiya's earlier
linear-independence results \cite{lucatachiya2014independence}.

\section{Finite-support denominator periods}\label{sec:period}

The least common multiple of the selected exponents survives cancellation
as the multiplicative order of the base modulo the reduced denominator.

\begin{theorem}[the exact denominator period]\label{res:period}
Let $F\subseteq\Npos$ be finite and nonempty, let $b\ge2$ be an integer, and
let $D_F>0$ be the denominator of $X_F(b)$ in lowest terms.  Then $D_F$ is
coprime to $b$, and
\[
  \operatorname{ord}_{D_F}(b)=\lcm\{n:n\in F\}.
\]
If moreover $\lcm(F)\ge2$, then $\lcm(F)<D_F$.  We use
$\operatorname{ord}_1(b)=1$, so the statement includes $F=\{1\}$
at $b=2$.
\end{theorem}

Put $L=\operatorname{lcm}(F)$.  Clearing denominators gives
$D_F\mid b^L-1$, so the upper divisibility for the order is immediate.
For the reverse, fix a divisibility-maximal $n\in F$ with $n\ge2$ and
choose a prime $\ell\mid\Phi_n(b)$. With $e=v_\ell(b^n-1)$, the
cyclotomic fact in Section~\ref{app:elementary-details} gives
$\operatorname{ord}_{\ell^e}(b)=n$ for the full prime power $\ell^e$.
Every other selected exponent $m$ has $n\nmid m$, hence
$v_\ell(b^m-1)<e$.  The $n$th summand has uniquely smallest $\ell$-adic
valuation and cannot cancel.  Thus $\ell^e\mid D_F$ and
$n\mid\operatorname{ord}_{D_F}(b)$.  Taking all maximal selected exponents
proves the order statement; the size bound follows from
$\operatorname{ord}_{D_F}(b)\mid\varphi(D_F)<D_F$ when $L\ge2$.
The case $F=\{1\}$ has order one directly.

The unique-valuation argument also permits signs $\pm1$ on the finite
summands. This signed extension is not included in the formal statement.
The distinction between primes and prime powers is visible in
\[
 X_{\{2,3\}}(2)=\frac{10}{21},\qquad
 X_{\{2,6\}}(2)=\frac{22}{63}.
\]
In both examples $2$ has multiplicative order six modulo the denominator.
The first combines orders two and three; the second retains the
order-six prime power $9$, although no prime divisor of $63$ has order six.
The boundary $F=\{1\}$ at base two has $D_F=L=1$.
These lower denominator bounds give no upper height control for infinite
partial sums and do not decide an infinite-support value.  Van Assche instead constructs approximants for the full Lambert series and proves
both nonvanishing and decay of the associated integer linear forms
\cite[Lemma~1 and (34)--(35)]{vanassche2001}.  That approximation mechanism
does not follow from denominator survival alone.


In particular, $1/21$ is not a finite subseries sum. If it were, the order
of $2$ modulo $21$ would force every selected exponent to divide $6$.
The exponent $1$ is excluded since its weight is $1$. Any sum containing
$2$ or $3$ exceeds $1/21$, whereas the only nonzero remaining sum is
$1/63$, from the exponent $6$. This will distinguish finite and infinite
representations in the next appendix.

\section{Rational membership}\label{sec:rational-membership}
The preceding results start from a support and prove irrationality.
We now fix a target and ask whether any support represents it.
The first recurrence is a necessary condition on a rational value;
the greedy recurrence later gives an exact membership criterion.
Neither supplies the missing arithmetic information for $1/2$ or $1/21$.

\subsection{Rational values and scaled tails}\label{sec:forced}
Suppose $X_A(2)=p/v$, where $p\in\Z$ and $v\ge1$ is an integer.
Multiplying the coefficient-series identity by $v2^N$ gives
\[
 z_N:=v\sum_{r\ge1}c_A(N+r)2^{-r}
     =2^Np-v\sum_{n=1}^{N}c_A(n)2^{N-n}\in\Z.
\]
Separating the first term of the tail then gives
$z_{N+1}=2z_N-vc_A(N+1)$.
All the coefficients $c_A(n)$ are divisor counts of the same set $A$.

For nonempty $A$, every $a_0=\min A$ consecutive integers contain
a multiple of $a_0$, so zero runs of $c_A$ have length at most $a_0-1$.
For infinite $A$, choose $k$ exponents and a common multiple $L$.
Then $c_A(L)\ge k$, and the scaled tail satisfies
$\sum_{r\ge1}c_A(L-1+r)2^{-r}\ge k/2$. Thus scaled tails are
unbounded.

The compatibility condition on the coefficients is expressed by
Dirichlet convolution:
$\mu*c_A=\mathbf1_A$, where $\mu$ is the M\"obius function.
A putative recurrence with integral forcing must therefore satisfy
$(\mu*c_A)(n)\in\{0,1\}$ for all $n$.
The telescoping proof of the integer-recurrence criterion and the
M\"obius inversion argument are given under
\papersectionlink{erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface.pdf}{record257:coefficient-recurrence}
{Bounds for a general coefficient sequence} in the companion paper.  The example $A=\{2\}$ there has value $1/3$.
The correspondence permits finite supports; infinitude remains a separate
requirement for a counterexample to Problem~\ref{res:problem}.

\subsection{The achievement set}\label{sec:geometry}
Let $w_n=(2^n-1)^{-1}$ and
\[
 \Ach=\left\{\sum_{n\ge1}\varepsilon_nw_n:
                   \varepsilon_n\in\{0,1\}\right\},\qquad
 R_N=\sum_{n>N}w_n.
\]
The estimate
\[
 2^{-N}<R_N\le2^{-N}+\frac23\,4^{-N}<w_N\qquad(N\ge1)
\]
follows by writing $w_n=2^{-n}+4^{-n}/(1-2^{-n})$ and using
$n\ge N+1\ge2$ for the middle bound. If two selectors first differ
at $n$, their sums differ by at least $w_n-R_n>0$, proving uniqueness.
Since every weight exceeds its tail, Hornich's theorem~\cite{hornich1941}, as proved by
Nitecki~\cite[Theorem~4(1), p.~9]{nitecki2013}, shows that the coding image is
a Cantor set of measure $\lim_N2^NR_N$; the estimate above gives
$2^NR_N\to1$, so $\lambda(\Ach)=1$.
Concretely, fixing the first $N$ digits gives $2^N$ disjoint closed
intervals of length $R_N$.  These interval unions decrease to $\Ach$,
and continuity of Lebesgue measure from above gives the same limit.
Kova\v{c}--Tao record this strict-tail inequality and the Cantor conclusion in the fixed-base setting~\cite[Remark~4.1]{kovactao}.
The
\papersectionlink{erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface.pdf}{record257:geometry}
{geometry section of the companion paper} also treats restricted supports.
For any allowed set $J$, removing exponents can only decrease the tail
of each retained weight, so the same inequality gives injectivity. If $J$ omits exactly the
finite set $F$, its achievement set has measure $2^{-|F|}$; if $J$
omits infinitely many exponents, that measure is zero. The
\href{https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/c91562bd574a387cde904481e609c7b4cacebb14/lean/ErdosProblems/Erdos257/MersenneSubseriesRigidity.lean\#L30}{tail comparison},
\href{https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/c91562bd574a387cde904481e609c7b4cacebb14/lean/ErdosProblems/Erdos257/MersenneSubseriesRigidity.lean\#L54}{injectivity} and
\href{https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/c91562bd574a387cde904481e609c7b4cacebb14/lean/ErdosProblems/Erdos257/MersenneSubseriesRigidity.lean\#L397}{measure dichotomy} have separate source statements.

\subsection{The greedy recurrence}\label{sec:actual-repairs}
For $x\ge0$, the greedy rule starts with $r_0=x$ and, at rank $n\ge1$,
selects $n$ when $r_{n-1}\ge(2^n-1)^{-1}$, subtracting that weight if
selected.  Let $A_x$ be the resulting support and
$c_x(n)=\#\{a\in A_x:a\mid n\}$.  Set
\[
 P_0=0,\qquad P_{N+1}=2P_N+c_x(N+1),\qquad
 Q_N=\lfloor2^Nx\rfloor-P_N.
\]
Here $P_N=\sum_{j=1}^N2^{N-j}c_x(j)$ truncates the coefficient
series~\eqref{eq:incidence}, not the selected Lambert weights.
Thus $Q_N$ measures coefficient truncation, whereas $r_N$ is the
real remainder after $N$ greedy decisions. The bound
$P_N\le2^NX_{A_x}(2)\le2^Nx$ gives $Q_N\ge0$, and
\begin{equation}
 Q_{N+1}=2Q_N+\beta_N-c_x(N+1),\qquad
 \beta_N=\lfloor2^{N+1}x\rfloor-2\lfloor2^Nx\rfloor\in\{0,1\}.
 \label{eq:actual-repair-recurrence}
\end{equation}

The recurrence is integral for every real target. Write
$\delta=x-X_{A_x}(2)\ge0$. The coefficient expansion gives
\[
 Q_N=\left\lfloor 2^N\delta+
             \sum_{r\ge1}c_x(N+r)2^{-r}\right\rfloor.
\]
For a represented target, $\delta=0$ and $Q_N=O(\sqrt N)$, leaving
too little room for unit increases throughout a long window.
For an unrepresented target, $2^N\delta$ eventually dominates the
divisor count in the recurrence and forces strict increase.


\begin{theorem}[membership and nonincreasing integer remainders]\label{res:general-repair}
For every real $x\ge0$, the following are equivalent:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 x\in\Ach;\\
 \forall K\ge0\ \exists N\ge K:\quad Q_{N+1}\le Q_N;\\
 \forall K\ge0\ \exists N\in[K,K+2\lfloor\sqrt K\rfloor+12):
 \quad Q_{N+1}\le Q_N.
 \end{gathered}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For a represented target, the remaining sum is at least $w_n$ exactly
when $n$ is selected, since $R_n<w_n$. Hence the greedy rule recovers
the support, and
\[
 0\le Q_N\le\sum_{r\ge1}c_x(N+r)2^{-r}
 \le2\sqrt N+4,
\]
since $c_x(n)\le\tau(n)\le2\sqrt n$ and
$\sqrt{N+r}\le\sqrt N+\sqrt r\le\sqrt N+r$.
Put $s=\lfloor\sqrt K\rfloor$ and $T=2s+12$.
Strict increase at all $T$ steps would imply $Q_{K+T}\ge T$.
But $K+T<(s+4)^2$ gives $Q_{K+T}<2s+12=T$.
This proves the window condition and hence cofinal nonincreases.

Conversely, if $x\notin\Ach$, then $\delta>0$ and
$Q_N\ge2^N\delta-1$, which eventually exceeds
$c_x(N+1)\le N+1$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:actual-repair-recurrence} then makes $Q_N$ strictly
increasing, contradicting cofinal nonincreases.
\end{proof}

The nonincreases must occur along the target's own greedy sequence.
For $x=0$, no exponent is selected and $Q_N=0$ at every rank.  A finite subseries sum is likewise represented and satisfies the
criterion.  The target $x=3/4$ lies strictly between $R_1<2/3$ and
$w_1=1$, so it is not represented and its integer remainders eventually
increase strictly.  For $1/2$ and $1/21$, the theorem does not establish
which alternative occurs.

An ordinary extension gives a uniform subpower window: for each
$0<\varepsilon<1$, its length is
$\lceil C_\varepsilon(K+1)^\varepsilon\rceil$ for a suitable constant
$C_\varepsilon$. The linked formal proof establishes the square-root window.
Indeed, $\tau(n)\le A_\varepsilon n^\varepsilon$ gives
$Q_N\le D_\varepsilon(N+1)^\varepsilon$ for represented targets,
where $D_\varepsilon=A_\varepsilon\sum_{r\ge1}r^\varepsilon2^{-r}$.
Choose $C_\varepsilon>D_\varepsilon(C_\varepsilon+3)^\varepsilon$,
which is possible because $\varepsilon<1$.
For $T=\lceil C_\varepsilon(K+1)^\varepsilon\rceil$, strict increase
at all $T$ steps would give
\[
 T\le Q_{K+T}\le D_\varepsilon(K+T+1)^\varepsilon
 \le D_\varepsilon(C_\varepsilon+3)^\varepsilon(K+1)^\varepsilon<T,
\]
a contradiction. The converse still follows from exponential growth
when $x$ is not represented. The shorter window does not decide
membership of a specified target.

At $x=1/2$, the digits $\beta_N$ vanish for $N\ge1$; at $x=1/21$ they
are six-periodic.  Thus the unresolved arithmetic input is
\begin{equation}
 \forall K\ \exists N\ge K:\qquad
 c_x(N+1)\ge Q_N+\beta_N,
 \qquad x\in\{1/2,1/21\}.
 \label{eq:actual-selector-obligation}
\end{equation}
Both $Q_N$ and $c_x$ must arise from the same greedy support $A_x$.
Counterexamples to fixed-multiplier schedules, with their finite phase
masks, are retained in the companion paper. They concern those schedules;
they do not decide either target.

\section{Integer quotients, approximation and further questions}\label{sec:open}
For $1/21$ we compare integer greedy remainders with the real greedy
sequence; for $1/2$ we allow arbitrary finite approximating supports.
Both tests require suitable data at unbounded depths.

\paragraph{Integer quotients for $1/21$.}
For $M,d\ge1$, set
\[
 q_M(d)=\left\lfloor\frac{2^M}{2^d-1}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad T_M=\left\lfloor\frac{2^M}{21}\right\rfloor.
\]
For $d\ge2$, the geometric expansion gives
$q_M(d)=\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor M/d\rfloor}2^{M-jd}$: the omitted fraction
$2^{M\bmod d}/(2^d-1)$ is less than $1$. Thus $q_M(d)$ is the
coefficient prefix contributed by exponent $d$.
Starting with remainder $T_{2R}$, consider $d=2,\ldots,R$ in order and
subtract $q_{2R}(d)$ whenever it does not exceed the current remainder.  Let $D_R$ be the set of selected exponents and $s_R$ the final
remainder.  Thus
\[
 s_R=T_{2R}-\sum_{d\in D_R}q_{2R}(d)\ge0.
\]
The precision is $4^R$, but $D_R$ records decisions only through
rank $R$. The agreement condition below also uses a second run at
that same precision, continued through rank $2R$.
For example, $R=6$ gives $T_{12}=195$, $D_6=\{5\}$ and
$s_6=195-\lfloor4096/31\rfloor=63\le64$.  This is one row satisfying
the bound below, not evidence that such rows occur at unbounded depths.


Write $r_n=r_n(1/21)$ for the real greedy remainder and $A_{1/21}$ for its
support.  The condition $\mathcal F_{21}$ means that there exist integers
$n,R_0,K_0\ge0$ with all of the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $r_n>R_n$, the set of positive exponents outside $A_{1/21}$ is
finite, and every exponent greater than $n$ belongs to $A_{1/21}$;
\item for every $R\ge R_0$, the integer rule with target $T_{2R}$ and
weights $q_{2R}(2),\ldots,q_{2R}(2R)$ selects exactly the same exponents
as the real greedy rule on $\{2,\ldots,2R\}$;
\item for every $K\ge K_0$, the interval $(K,2K]$ contains an exponent
of $A_{1/21}$.
\end{enumerate}
A positive limiting remainder gives a tail violation and eventual
selection of every exponent, hence the first and last clauses.
The middle clause additionally requires agreement with the integer rules.

\begin{theorem}[integer-quotient tests for $1/21$]
\label{res:one-over-twenty-one-frontier}
The following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $1/21\in\Ach$ if and only if $\mathcal F_{21}$ does not hold.
\item If there is an unbounded sequence of ranks $R$ with $s_R\le 2^R$,
  then $1/21\in\Ach$.
\item On $\mathcal F_{21}$, eventually $s_R>2^R$, the boundary rank $R+1$
  belongs to $D_{R+1}$, and, for all sufficiently large $R$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 D_{R+1}&=D_R\cup\{R+1\},\\
 s_{R+1}&=4s_R+
 \left\lfloor\frac{4(2^{2R}\bmod21)}{21}\right\rfloor
 -2c_{D_R}(2R+1)-c_{D_R}(2R+2)\\
 &\hspace{3em}{}-(2^{R+1}+1).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here $c_{D_R}(m)=\#\{d\in D_R:d\mid m\}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $x=1/21$, $G=A_{1/21}$ and $\delta=x-X_G(2)\ge0$.
If $x\notin\Ach$, then $\delta>0$. The real remainder tends to
$\delta$, so every sufficiently small weight is selected and eventually
$r_n>R_n$. For the integer comparisons, first choose $d_0$ with $w_d<\delta/2$
for $d>d_0$. Comparisons through $d_0$ are strict,
since equality would give a finite representation of $x$.
After division by $4^R$, each quotient weight differs from $w_d$ by
less than $4^{-R}$, and the remainders differ by at most $d/4^R$
whenever earlier decisions agree. For large $R$, the first $d_0$
decisions therefore agree. At later ranks $d\le2R$, the normalised
remainder exceeds $\delta/2>w_d$, since $2R/4^R<\delta/2$;
both rules select every remaining rank through $2R$. This proves $\mathcal F_{21}$. A represented target has
$r_n\le R_n$ at every rank, giving the converse in (1).

For every $R$, the rounding errors satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \left|x-X_{D_R}(2)-\frac{s_R}{4^R}\right|
 \le\frac{R+1}{4^R}.
 \label{eq:twenty-one-rounding}
\end{equation}
Thus $s_R\le2^R$ at unbounded ranks gives finite subseries sums
tending to $x$. Closedness of $\Ach$ proves (2), without compatibility
between the sets $D_R$; Section~\ref{sec:period} excludes a finite
representation.

On $\mathcal F_{21}$, the eventual agreement gives
$D_R=G\cap\{2,\ldots,R\}$ and $D_{R+1}=D_R\cup\{R+1\}$.
The rounding bound implies $s_R/4^R\to\delta>0$.
Finally, for $d\in D_R$ (so $d\ge2$), use
$q_{M+2}(d)=4q_M(d)+2\mathbf1_{d\mid M+1}+\mathbf1_{d\mid M+2}$,
together with the analogous target identity and
$q_{2R+2}(R+1)=2^{R+1}+1$, to obtain (3).
The full comparison induction and both quotient identities are given in
\papersectionlink{erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface.pdf}{record257:twenty-one-quotients}
{the companion paper's integer-quotient proof for $1/21$}.
\end{proof}


\noindent In the list $q_{2R}(2),\ldots,q_{2R}(R)$, each weight exceeds
the sum of its successors by at least $2^R+1$. Distinct subset sums
are therefore separated by more than $2^R$, and the greedy sum is the
largest not exceeding the target. Thus, if
$D\subseteq\{2,\ldots,R\}$ and an integer $s$ satisfy
$\sum_{d\in D}q_{2R}(d)+s=T_{2R}$ with $0\le s\le2^R$, then
$D=D_R$ and $s=s_R$
(\mword{Erdos249257/TwentyOneQuotientGreedy.lean}{231}{twentyOneClosedRow_forces_quotientGreedy}{uniqueness of a finite representation with the stated remainder bound}).
The cited finite crossing lemmas give additional consequences under their
alignment hypotheses: an earlier finite prefix cannot occur, and a real
greedy exponent must be skipped
(\mword{Erdos249257/TwentyOneQuotientGreedy.lean}{5179}{twentyOneAlignedSaturatedCrossing_forces_canonical_ancestor_hole}{the missing-prefix consequence of an aligned crossing},
\mword{Erdos249257/TwentyOneQuotientGreedy.lean}{5223}{twentyOneAlignedSaturatedCrossing_forces_scaled_greedy_skip}{the real greedy skip forced by that crossing}).

\paragraph{Approximation to $1/2$ by finite supports.}
For $A\subseteq\{2,\ldots,M\}$ and $1\le m\le M$, define the integer
\[
 K_A(m)=2^{m-1}-\sum_{j=2}^{m}2^{m-j}c_A(j).
\]
It measures the error in the truncated divisor-coefficient sum, after
multiplication by $2^m$.  In particular,
$K_A(1)=1$ and $K_A(m+1)=2K_A(m)-c_A(m+1)$.

\begin{theorem}[finite approximations with vanishing scaled error]
\label{res:terminalhalf}
Suppose there are integers $M_j\ge1$ tending to infinity and sets
$A_j\subseteq\{2,\ldots,M_j\}$ such that
\[
 \frac{|K_{A_j}(M_j)|}{2^{M_j}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Then $X_A(2)=1/2$ for some infinite set $A\subseteq\Npos$.
\end{theorem}

Only the terminal coefficient error needs control: the omitted tail
has the uniform bound below. Neither agreement between the supports
$A_j$ nor bounds on earlier values of $K_{A_j}$ are required:
\[
 \left|X_{A_j}(2)-\frac12\right|
 \le \frac{|K_{A_j}(M_j)|+2\sqrt{M_j}+4}{2^{M_j}}.
\]
Indeed, $c_{A_j}(n)\le\tau(n)\le2\sqrt n$ and
$\sqrt{M+r}\le\sqrt M+r$ bound the normalised tail by
$\sum_{r\ge1}2^{-r}(2\sqrt M+2r)=2\sqrt M+4$.
Thus $X_{A_j}(2)\to1/2$. Closedness of $\Ach$ gives a representing
support; the odd reduced denominators of finite sums make it infinite.
An $O(\sqrt{M_j})$ terminal error suffices, but any $o(2^{M_j})$
error is allowed.  For a finite $D\subseteq\{2,\ldots,M\}$, the
floor-quotient identity gives
\[
 K_D(M)=2^{M-1}-\sum_{d\in D}
                \left\lfloor\frac{2^M}{2^d-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
The exact quotient rows considered in the companion paper satisfy
$\sum_{d\in D}q_M(d)=2^{M-1}-1$, so they have $K_D(M)=1$.
The terminal criterion allows a larger error of either sign. At a fixed depth these are
different conditions, although cofinal existence of either kind of
approximation characterises $1/2\in\Ach$.

Conversely, if $X_A(2)=1/2$, then $1\notin A$, and the prefixes
$A_M=A\cap\{2,\ldots,M\}$ satisfy
\[
 K_{A_M}(M)=\sum_{r\ge1}c_A(M+r)2^{-r}
       \le 2\sqrt M+4.
\]
The right-hand side uses the full support $A$: truncation leaves its
coefficients through $M$ unchanged. Thus the existence hypothesis of
Theorem~\ref{res:terminalhalf} is equivalent to $1/2\in\Ach$.
Existence at unbounded depths remains unproved; establishing it would
refute Problem~\ref{res:problem}.

\paragraph{Finite families with a shared prefix.}
Put $B(m)=2\lfloor\sqrt m\rfloor+4$.  For $0\le K\le M$, consider a
family $A_1,\ldots,A_{B(M)}\subseteq\{2,\ldots,M\}$ with
\[
 1\le K_{A_k}(m)\le B(m)\quad(1\le m\le M),
 \qquad K_{A_k}(M)=k.
\]
Require that all the $A_k$ agree on $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ and that some
integer $E\ge B(M)$ satisfies
\[
 \sum_{j=K+1}^{M}1_{A_k}(j)\,2^{M-j}+k=E
 \qquad(1\le k\le B(M)).
\]
Thus the binary suffixes have consecutive values $E-k$. The hypothesis
asks for a whole family at each available depth, not merely one
approximant.

\begin{theorem}[unbounded shared-prefix families represent one half]
\label{res:cylinderhalf}
Suppose that for every $N$ there are $M,K$ with
$\max\{N,1\}\le M$, $0\le K\le M$, and a family satisfying all the
conditions in the preceding paragraph.  Then $X_A(2)=1/2$ for some
infinite set $A\subseteq\Npos$.
\end{theorem}

At each available depth $M$, choose the member with terminal carry
$1$. Its scaled terminal error is $2^{-M}$, so
Theorem~\ref{res:terminalhalf} applies along unbounded depths. The other
shared-prefix conditions are not used in this compactness step.
No construction at unbounded depths is established here.

The tests above leave three kinds of arithmetic information to be
supplied: returns of the actual greedy sequence, finite approximants at
unbounded depths, or an exclusion of a possible final skip. The following
questions specify those missing inputs.

\begin{problem}[membership of 1/21 in the Mersenne achievement set]
\label{prob:one-over-twenty-one-membership}
For the greedy remainder of $1/21$, prove that arbitrarily large $N$
satisfy
\[
 2^{N+1}r_N(1/21)<\frac{2^{N+1}}{2^{N+1}-1},
 \quad\text{equivalently}\quad
 r_N(1/21)<\frac1{2^{N+1}-1}.
\]
Equivalently, exclude the condition $\mathcal F_{21}$ defined above.
One sufficient route is to rule out the eventual recurrence in
Theorem~\ref{res:one-over-twenty-one-frontier}(3) together with $s_R>2^R$;
another is to prove $s_R\le2^R$ at arbitrarily large ranks.  Neither
sufficient route is claimed to be necessary by itself.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[bounded returns of the scaled remainder]\label{prob:scaled-return}
For each of the targets $x=1/2$ and $x=1/21$, does the greedy remainder
$r_N(x)$ return to one bounded interval after scaling by $2^N$?
\[
 \exists B<\infty\ \forall K\ \exists N\ge K:
 \qquad 2^N r_N(x)\le B.
\]
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[arithmetic tests for the greedy sequence]\label{prob:actual-invariant}
Can a finite-memory, $2$-adic or discrepancy argument prove $s_R\le2^R$
at arbitrarily large ranks, or rule out the eventual recurrence in
Theorem~\ref{res:one-over-twenty-one-frontier}(3)?  Such an argument must use
the divisor counts of the actual greedy support.  Can a bounded window of
$R\bmod6$, residues of $s_R$, endpoint divisor counts and the finite set of
eventual skips force a decrease or a contradiction?  Alternatively, can one
show that these bounded-memory data cannot distinguish the actual sequence
from sequences that remain above $2^R$ but need not come from a support?
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[final-skip Diophantine exclusion]\label{prob:fatal-interval}
Let $E=\sum_{n\ge1}(2^n-1)^{-1}$.  If $1/21\notin\Ach$, let $M$ be the last
skipped exponent, $S_M$ its finite skipped prefix, and
\[
 a_M=\frac1{21}+\sum_{d\in S_M}\frac1{2^d-1}.
\]
Write $\operatorname{gap}_M=(2^M-1)^{-1}-R_M>0$.
Can the arithmetic restrictions on this last skipped exponent be used to
prove $|E-a_M|\ge\operatorname{gap}_M$, contradicting
\[
 0<a_M-E<\operatorname{gap}_M?
\]
\end{problem}


\section{Elementary details used in the proofs}\label{app:elementary-details}
\paragraph{Cyclotomic prime-power fact.}
Let $b\ge2$, $n\ge2$, $\ell\mid\Phi_n(b)$ be prime and
$e=v_\ell(b^n-1)$.  Then $\operatorname{ord}_{\ell^e}(b)=n$.
We include the $2$-adic case.
For odd $\ell$, put $d=\operatorname{ord}_{\ell}(b)$ and
$s=v_\ell(b^d-1)$.  The elementary lifting identity
$v_\ell(b^{dt}-1)=s+v_\ell(t)$ follows by factoring a geometric sum
when $\ell\nmid t$ and by a binomial expansion for a factor $\ell$.
In the factorisation $b^n-1=\prod_{r\mid n}\Phi_r(b)$, subtracting
these valuations over proper divisors gives
\[
 v_\ell(\Phi_n(b))=
 \begin{cases}s&n=d,\\1&n=d\ell^j,\ j\ge1,\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
If $n=d$, no smaller positive exponent gives $b^m\equiv1\pmod\ell$.
If $n=d\ell^j$, the full valuation is $e=s+j$; the same lifting
identity shows that the least exponent giving valuation $e$ is
$d\ell^j=n$.
For $\ell=2$, $b$ is odd.  Factoring $b^{2t}-1$ gives
\[
 v_2(b^{2^j}-1)=v_2(b-1)+v_2(b+1)+j-1\qquad(j\ge1).
\]
The only possible indices $n\ge2$ are $n=2^j$:
$v_2(\Phi_2(b))=v_2(b+1)$ and
$v_2(\Phi_{2^j}(b))=1$ for $j\ge2$; all other indices have
valuation zero.  The displayed identity again makes $2^j$ the least
exponent with the full valuation.  This proves the fact.
Finally $\Phi_n(b)>1$: each primitive $n$th root $\zeta$ satisfies
$|b-\zeta|>1$, and their product is $\Phi_n(b)$.

\paragraph{Exact scalar cover cost.}
For $t\ge1$, put $z=\log_2t$.  The substitution $y=2^\alpha$
reduces the infimum defining $\Psi(t)$ to $y^z/(y-1)$ on $1<y\le2$.
Its derivative has the sign of $(z-1)y-z$.  Hence
\[
 \Psi(t)=
 \begin{cases}t,&1\le t\le4,\\
 z^z/(z-1)^{z-1},&t>4.
 \end{cases}
\]
The minimum is at $\alpha=1$ for $t\le4$ and in the interior for $t>4$;
the quotient diverges as $\alpha\downarrow0$. This scalar identity does
not supply a converse to the positive-cover criterion.

\subsection*{The cost for a finite set of divisors}
For the following finite divisor sets, the lower bound is asymptotically
attained. Here $K_*(F)$ is the infimum of the cost $K$ from
Section~\ref{sec:comparison} over finite or countable covers of $F$, their majorants and exponents,
and positive weights of total one. A one-set cover therefore has weight
$1$, without the dyadic index factor in (V).
For $F(q,P)=\{qd:d\mid\prod_{p\in P}p\}$, where $q\ge2$ and no $p\in P$
divides $q$, put $S=\sum_{p\in P}1/p$.  If $S\ge1$, then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{e(S-1)}q\le K_*\bigl(F(q,P)\bigr)\le\frac{eS}q.
 \label{eq:optimal-cube-cost}
\end{equation}
For the lower bound, we condition on $q\mid n$ and write
$f_F(n)=2^Z$.  The Chinese remainder theorem gives
$\mathbb EZ=S$.  For $z\ge0$ and $v=\alpha\log2>0$,
\[
 \frac{2^{\alpha z}}{2^\alpha-1}
 \ge\frac{e^{(z-1)v}}v\ge e(z-1)\quad(z>1);
\]
for $0\le z\le1$ the claimed lower bound is nonpositive.
Thus $\Psi(2^z)\ge e(z-1)$; averaging and multiplying by the
density $1/q$ gives the lower bound. For the upper bound, use the
one-set cover with $z=1/S$ and
$\alpha=\log_2(1+z)$; its exact positive expansion has cost
\[
 \frac1{qz}\prod_{p\in P}(1+z/p)\le\frac{eS}q.
\]
In particular,
$1-1/S\le qK_*(F(q,P))/(eS)\le1$.
Thus $K_*(F(q,P))\sim eS/q$ as $S\to\infty$, uniformly over the
permitted choices of $q$ and $P$.

\section{Sources, verification and reproducibility}\label{app:sources}

\evidenceparagraph{\evidencerecordurl}

For Erd\H{o}s's reciprocal-summable extension and fractional-part
argument, see pp.~222 and 226 of \cite{erdos1968}. The periodic theorem
\cite{lucatachiya2014periodic} is also stated in Luca and Tachiya's account~\cite[Theorem~A and Example~2, pp.~139--140]{lucatachiya2017},
and Hornich's strict-tail theorem is proved in Nitecki's exposition
\cite[Theorem~4(1)]{nitecki2013}. These expositions are the sources used
here for those two results; the original articles were not independently
retrieved.  The \emph{Formal Conjectures}
file~\cite{formalconjectures257} is statement-level prior art, not a
proof dependency.

Formal bindings concern statements, not every printed argument. The mixed
implication has a formal proof; a separate formal construction of a

construction, Corollary~\ref{res:strict-mixed-supports}, signed

have ordinary arguments here, without independent human review. The

No historical priority is asserted for the support comparison.

\paragraph{Reproducing the weighted theorem.}
The two declarations for Theorem~\ref{res:weighted-support} are in
the public source at
\href{https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/tree/91ca3405b795a520825ac5ca04dcd591b9ddf3e3}{commit \texttt{91ca3405}}.

python3 scripts/lean_fast_build.py --jobs 2 \

The cache download is optional.  The modules contain

excerpts.text:
Part~I proves that $\sum_{a\in A}(b^a-1)^{-1}$ is irrational for every
integer $b\ge2$ and every infinite $A\subseteq E\cup V$ under two
hypotheses. The set $E$ satisfies a finite-prime weighted summability
condition at base two, while $V$ admits a summable positive divisor cover.
The estimates for the two sets hold on one finite distribution, so the
union criterion reaches supports lying in neither individual class.
The record also develops finite-denominator arithmetic, achievement-set
geometry and integer-quotient tests for $1/2$ and $1/21$. Conditional
arguments retain their hypotheses, computations their finite ranges, and
counterexamples the estimates they refute. Both rational targets and the
unrestricted base-two problem remain open.

\section*{Introduction}
For an integer $b\ge2$, the series $X_A(b)=\sum_{a\in A}(b^a-1)^{-1}$
is irrational for several classes of infinite supports $A$. Erd\H{o}s proved the full-support case
and later stated a criterion assuming only convergence of
$\sum_{a\in A}1/a$; the periodic-support results belong to Luca and
Tachiya. We begin with these antecedents and prove two hereditary
criteria which also admit supports of divergent reciprocal sum.
The proofs subtract an explicitly chosen integer from $(b^N-1)X_A(b)$,
leaving a positive difference $\Delta_{b,A}(N)$. If $X_A(b)=p/q$ with
$q>0$, then $q\Delta_{b,A}(N)\in\mathbb Z$, so
$\Delta_{b,A}(N)\ge1/q$. We rule out rationality by making this
difference arbitrarily small. In a finite average, the incomplete residue periods produce an error
without the factor $1/a$ needed for summation over exponents. Averaging
again over dyadic lengths restores this factor. The decisive point for the
union theorem is stronger than proving the two criteria separately: both
errors are controlled on the same finite distribution, and one index is
chosen only after they have been added. Keeping the modulus dependence
explicit makes that common distribution available to the cover estimate.

Part~I gives the support theorems and the proofs followed by the short
paper, \emph{Irrationality criteria for Lambert subseries}.
The subsequent parts concern a different question: whether a prescribed
rational number belongs to the Mersenne achievement set. The finite
identities in Sections~5--8 describe the integer quotients and their
relation to the real greedy sequence. Sections~9--12 state the additional
uniform or unbounded-depth assertions needed to apply them. Notation
specific to a recurrence is introduced with that recurrence.

Section~13 returns to the support criteria. A logarithmic divisor cost
cannot uniformly replace the fractional-cover cost when sampling on
multiples of a prescribed modulus, even over complete periods. We prove
the counterexample and an initial-interval estimate that survives it.

None of these arguments decides the universal problem, half-membership
or $1/21$-membership. The conditional results specify sufficient
hypotheses or equivalent membership conditions, and the computations
cover only the stated finite ranges. Each counterexample concerns the
particular estimate under discussion.

\section{Limitations of the recorded methods}
\label{sec:257-wall}
A bound for the actual greedy sequence and a bound uniform over a class
of supports are different assertions. The following examples separate
those assertions, starting with uniqueness at a fixed target. They
exclude the specified estimates or their proposed uniformity, without
giving an obstruction to every possible method.

\subsection{Comparison of the remaining inputs}

Route~4 packages recorded equivalences; it does not establish their
unproved existence hypotheses.  Route~3 must be compared with the external
prime-support theorem of Tao and Ter\"av\"ainen
\cite[Theorem~1.3]{taoteravainen2025}; reproducing it in this framework
requires its own analytic input.  Route~2 offers a different finite
search space under the conditions stated there.  Routes~1 and~5 share
some incidence identities, but this is not a proof that every missing
hypothesis is equivalent.  The appropriate comparison is the input each
route needs, its quantifiers, and what a successful estimate would imply.

\subsubsection*{Filling the remaining binary positions}

\begin{thm}[Filling the remaining binary positions]\label{record:257bm-c7}
For any $c\ge4$ and any finite $D\subseteq[2,c)$ with $\mathrm{value}(D)<1/2$ and the sharp
capacity
\[
\ensuremath{S}(D,1,2c-2) < 2^{c-2},
\]
there is an exact row $E$ at endpoint $2c-2$ with $D\subseteq E$ and every new rank strictly
above $c$. The implication requires the displayed capacity bound,
but neither a crossing condition nor a specified real greedy prefix.
The crossing hypothesis used in Theorem~\ref{record:257bm-c4} is
one way to seek that input, not an additional premise of this filling
result.  No strict comparison between the corresponding cofinal
existence statements is asserted.
\end{thm}

\begin{thm}[An exact sum at depth $2c-2$]\label{record:257bm-c8}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{record:257bm-c7}, there is a
set $E\subseteq\{2,\ldots,2c-2\}$ with
\[
 Q(E,2c-2)=2^{2c-3}-1.
\]
This conclusion forgets the additional support-extension information
in that theorem.  It is the form used when only the existence of an
exact row is needed.
\end{thm}

\begin{prop}[Quotients in the upper half of the index range]\label{record:257bm-c9}
For integers $d\ge2$ and $d\le M<2d$,
\[
 q(M,d)=\left\lfloor\frac{2^M}{2^d-1}\right\rfloor=2^{M-d}.
\]
Indeed, the quotient is $2^{M-d}+2^{M-d}/(2^d-1)$, whose second
term is strictly between zero and one.  In
Theorem~\ref{record:257bm-c7}, the available ranks
$d=c+1,\ldots,2c-2$ therefore supply the binary weights
$2^{c-3},\ldots,1$.  They represent every integer from $0$ to
$2^{c-2}-1$, which explains both the capacity bound and the
choice of terminal depth.
\end{prop}

\begin{thm}[A finite sum from a skipped prefix]\label{record:257bm-c10}
Let $c\ge4$ and $D\subseteq\{2,\ldots,c-1\}$ satisfy
\[
 0<\frac12-X_D(2)<\frac1{2^c-1}.
\]
Then there is $E$ with $D\subseteq E\subseteq\{2,\ldots,2c-2\}$ and
$Q(E,2c-2)=2^{2c-3}-1$.  No separate sharp-capacity assumption is
required.  The binary completion in the linked proof uses ranks
$c,\ldots,2c-2$; it may therefore insert $c$.
Theorem~\ref{record:257bm-c7} instead assumes the sharper
$(c-2)$-bit bound so that every added rank is strictly greater than $c$.
\end{thm}

For a finite $F\subseteq\{2,\ldots,n\}$ with $X_F(2)>1/2$, take
$c$ to be its first crossing rank and $D=F\cap\{2,\ldots,c-1\}$.
Then $c\ge4$ because $1/3+1/7<1/2$, and the displayed hypotheses
hold: equality at the lower endpoint is excluded by odd denominators.
The Lean proofs use the theorem in exactly this first-crossing form.

excerpts.text:
We study the running least common multiples of integers whose prime
factors belong to a fixed finite set.
For $\{2,3,5\}$, a five-map argument proves irrationality of the sum over
distinct running LCMs. Two-prime sums reduce to a transcendental Hecke--Mahler
value. For the repeated three-prime sum we give an equivalent residue
criterion, whose arithmetic condition remains open. Complete ordinary
arguments for general sums over distinct running LCMs and prime-power subseries are
retained as remarks awaiting formalisation.

excerpts.section: Two sums from running least common multiples
excerpts.text:
\section{Two sums from running least common multiples}\label{long269:sec:problem}
Let $P$ be a finite set of at least two primes, and let $\mathcal S_P$
consist of $1$ and all positive integers whose prime factors belong to
$P$. For $x\ge1$, put
\[
 \Lprefix(x)=\lcm\{u\in\mathcal S_P:u\le x\},\qquad
 \hgt_P(x)=\prod_{p\in P}p^{\lfloor\log_p x\rfloor}.
\]
Every integer in this finite set divides $\hgt_P(x)$, and the set
contains the largest power of each prime in $P$ below or equal to $x$.
Their product therefore equals the least common multiple:
$\Lprefix(x)=\hgt_P(x)$. The value changes only at a positive prime
power. Summing its distinct reciprocals gives
\[
 \mathcal D_P=1+\sum_{\substack{t=p^n\\p\in P,\ n\ge1}}\frac1{\hgt_P(t)}.
\]
We begin with an irrationality result for three primes.

\begin{theorem}[the sum over distinct running LCMs at $\{2,3,5\}$]\label{long269:res:distinct-height-235}
The sum $\mathcal D_{\{2,3,5\}}$ is irrational.
\end{theorem}

The proof in Section~\ref{long269:sec:distinct-235} gives the primes three
different roles. Powers of $2$ delimit the blocks; powers of $5$ occur
often enough to separate the five affine tail images; powers of $3$
have an irrational block frequency. Separation makes each tail determine
the next block and tail. Under rationality there are only finitely many
tails, so repetition would force an impossible periodic block sequence.

Erd\H{o}s asserted the general conclusion for every finite $P$ with
$|P|\ge2$ in his letter of 1 January 1973, without printing a
proof~\cite[p.~335]{erdos1974letter}. The theorem above is a special case
of that assertion. The general argument in
Section~\ref{long269:sec:distinct-all} compares nearby tails and finds an
isolated interchange of jumps on a torus. We retain it as an ordinary
argument awaiting formalisation, with its intermediate claims stated as
remarks. The specialised five-map proof is independent of that argument.

The question in Erd\H{o}s Problem~\#269 retains multiplicities. If
$a_1<a_2<\cdots$ enumerates $\mathcal S_P$, it asks about
\[
 \mathcal R_P=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{[a_1,\ldots,a_n]}
             =\sum_{u\in\mathcal S_P}\frac1{\Lprefix(u)}
\]
\cite[p.~65]{erdosgraham1980}\cite[p.~106]{erdos1988}; the numbering is
Bloom's~\cite{erdosproblems}. For $P=\{2,3,5\}$, the integers $5$ and $6$
both have running LCM $60$. They contribute $2/60$ to $\mathcal R_P$ and
$1/60$ to $\mathcal D_P$. Thus Theorem~\ref{long269:res:distinct-height-235}
concerns the sum over distinct values, whereas the problem concerns
the sum with multiplicity. The arguments in this paper leave
$\mathcal R_P$ unresolved when $P$ is finite and $|P|\ge3$.

For two primes the conclusion is stronger.

\begin{theorem}[two-prime transcendence]\label{long269:res:lead-two-prime}
Let $p$ and $q$ be distinct primes.  Then $\mathcal R_{\{p,q\}}$ and
$\mathcal D_{\{p,q\}}$ are transcendental.
\end{theorem}
\evidenceremark{The Lean proof assumes the transcendence theorem of Bugeaud
and Laurent.}

Fan's post of 26 June 2026 gave the finite-prime running-LCM identity,
the factorisation of $\mathcal R_{\{p,q\}}$, and the Hecke--Mahler reduction
with its transcendence conclusion~\cite{fan2026comment}. We reproduce that
calculation in Section~\ref{long269:sec:two-prime}. Both values are
nonconstant polynomials over $\mathbb Q$ in one boundary sum, whose
transcendence follows from Loxton and van der Poorten
\cite[Theorem~8, p.~40]{loxtonvdp1977}, in the formulation of Bugeaud and
Laurent~\cite[Theorem~1.1]{bugeaudlaurent2023}. No priority is claimed for
this deduction.

Retaining multiplicities preserves the bases but changes the numerators.
The repeated tails satisfy $X_{a+1}=b_aX_a-m_a$, with
$b_a\in\{2,6,10,30\}$, while both $m_a$ and $X_a$ grow quadratically.
The preceding finite-tail repetition argument no longer applies. Rationality would
still make every sufficiently late $BX_a$ integral, where $B$ is the
denominator part coprime to $30$. A finite segment excludes such an
integer tail when its least positive residue exceeds the quadratic
bound. Irrationality is equivalent to finding these segments for every
$B$ beyond every prescribed onset. The finite computations do not
establish either unbounded quantifier.

The five-map proof comes first. Sections~\ref{long269:sec:lcm}
and~\ref{long269:sec:two-prime} then supply the running LCM geometry and
two-prime formulae. For general distinct sums,
Section~\ref{long269:sec:distinct-all} uses comparison of two tails rather
than recovery from one; the finite-state, subseries and linear-flow
extensions follow as ordinary arguments pending formalisation.
Section~\ref{long269:sec:rank} separates exact kernel rank from approximation.
For the repeated target, Sections~\ref{long269:sec:blocks}--\ref{long269:sec:escape}
derive the coefficients, bounds and residue criterion; the remaining
sections distinguish finite certificates from missing arithmetic inputs.
Section~\ref{long269:sec:proof-sources} records formal coverage. The
\href{erdos-269-three-prime-running-lcm.pdf\#r4-five-map-theorem}{short paper}
concentrates on the five-map theorem and the
\href{erdos-269-three-prime-running-lcm.pdf\#r4-repeated-criterion}{repeated-tail criterion}.

We use $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ for exponents and braces for fractional parts.
In the finite-geometry section and in the kernel calculation, $P=\{p,q,r\}$ consists
of three pairwise distinct primes, $\hgt=\hgt_P$, and
\[
 \Kernel(i,j,k)=\hgt(p^iq^jr^k)^{-1}.
\]
The other sections specify their prime sets separately. For $\{2,3,5\}$,
$\mathcal S_P$ consists of the usual $5$-smooth integers. This fixed support
differs from a varying smoothness bound in $\Psi(x,y)$
\cite{hildebrand1986}. Tijdeman and Meijer~\cite[Sections~1--4]{tijdemanmeijer1974}
and the two-prime study of Languasco, Luca, Moree and Togb\'e
\cite{languasco2025} give the relevant lattice-counting context; the
estimates below use no smooth-number density asymptotic or gap theorem.
Kova\v{c} and Tao~\cite{

\section{The remaining arithmetic questions}\label{long269:sec:open}
\papersectiontarget{r3-open}

The finite recursions are explicit; the missing step is to prove that
successful segments exist with the required unbounded quantifiers.
Weighted shifts preserve the value of the series, but preservation does
not supply cancellation. We calculate the surviving boundary terms,
then identify the extra hypotheses needed by integer-recurrence and
function-theoretic approaches. The irrationality of $S$ remains open here.

\section{Dependencies and remaining questions}
\label{sec:erdos-269-complete-family-map}
The table separates the established special cases from the ordinary
generalisations awaiting formalisation and the unresolved repeated-sum
condition. Exact kernel rank concerns separation of a function; the
residue criterion concerns a scalar sum and still needs arithmetic
existence for its segments.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.26\linewidth}p{0.64\linewidth}}
\hline
Result & Dependency and limit\\\hline
Running LCMs and intervals of constancy & Prime-power divisibility and unique factorisation.
Their geometry alone gives no irrationality statement.\\
Two-prime values & Earlier factorisation plus the cited external
Hecke--Mahler value theorem.  The reduction to that theorem is checked in
Lean; the theorem itself is a cited input (Section~\ref{long269:sec:coverage}).\\
Distinct values, every $P$ & Integrality of the scaled tails,
rearranged chains at a return of the logarithmic flow, Kronecker's theorem
and an Euler characteristic count on a two-dimensional subtorus.  Ordinary
proof checked by a second agent; no Lean proof.  It stops for the repeated sums because
their scaled tails are unbounded.\\
Prime-power subseries & The same two-tail comparison with the integer $f_p$
and a chain chosen near the origin of the torus; no two-wall lemma.
Ordinary proof checked by a second agent; no Lean proof.  Says nothing about the whole
repeated sum.\\
Distinct values, blocks & Dyadic blocks, finitely many affine maps with
disjoint images, integrality of the scaled tails and the irrationality of
$\log p/\log q$.  The theorem for $\{2,3,5\}$ is checked in Lean; the
general criterion has an ordinary proof, and
Remark~\ref{long269:res:distinct-height-sets} adds exact finite
computations.  No statement about the repeated sums.\\
Arbitrary-order rank & Diagonal rescaling, separate one-dimensional
densities and a staircase determinant; checked in Lean.\\
Tail recurrence & Counting the original multiplicities, normalising by
half the boundary running LCM, and convergence; an abstract recurrence would
not identify the sum.\\
Denominator reduction & A finite prefix with cleared denominators and
an upper bound for positive integer tails.  The first valid index is
determined exactly (Proposition~\ref{long269:res:exact-denominator}); checked
in Lean.\\
Residue criterion & The actual recurrence, a dominating bound and segment
products comparable to $8^h$; the inequality at arbitrarily late starts remains
unproved.\\
Weighted differences & Exact reindexing and the contributions of the
new boundary strips; integer enumeration checks the displayed
counterexample to third-difference cancellation.\\
Finite computations & Direct checks settle only their individual
segments.  The two large exclusions have published witnesses and exact
checkers, and the larger scan a published saved run; none is a theorem
input.\\\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
None of these results proves irrationality of the repeated sum
$\mathcal R_P$ for three or more primes.

% The three pure-power coordinates and the running height.
\newcommand{\hgt}{\operatorname{H}}
\newcommand{\Lprefix}{\operatorname{L}}
\newcommand{\Kernel}{\operatorname{K}}

\runninghead{Distinct running least common multiples}
\title{Distinct running least common multiples}
\subtitle{Affine tails and Erd\H{o}s Problem~\#269}
\author{Will Cook}
\date{July 2026; revised 6 October 2026}


% A local PDF link uses its destination name directly. The shared web-style
% helper would make hyperref emit the literal GoToR name "nameddest=...".
\newcommand{\longrecord}[2]{\href{erdos269-running-lcm-reasoning-surface.pdf\##1}{#2}}

\begin{document}
\maketitle
\noteprovenance

\begin{abstract}
We give a five-map proof that the reciprocals of the distinct running least
common multiples of the $5$-smooth integers have an irrational sum.
The spacing of powers of $5$ separates the affine tail images; rationality
would then force periodicity, contrary to the frequency of powers of $3$.
For the sum counted with multiplicity, the tails instead give an integer
recurrence and an equivalent residue criterion for irrationality. Proving
that criterion for the actual coefficients remains open here.
\end{abstract}

\section{Two sums from running least common multiples}\label{sec:problem}
Let $P$ be a finite set of primes and $\mathcal S_P$ the positive integers
with prime factors in $P$, including $1$. For $P=\{2,3,5\}$, the running
least common multiples of these $5$-smooth integers begin
$1,2,6,12,60,60,120,360,360,\ldots$. Put
\[
 \Lprefix(x)=\lcm\{u\in\mathcal S_P:u\le x\},\qquad
 \hgt_P(x)=\prod_{p\in P}p^{\lfloor\log_p x\rfloor}\quad(x\ge1).
\]
Every member of the prefix divides $\hgt_P(x)$, while the prefix contains
the largest power of each $p\in P$ at most $x$. Thus
$\Lprefix(x)=\hgt_P(x)$, with a jump by $p$ exactly at each positive
power of $p$. Counting distinct running LCMs or retaining multiplicities gives
\[
 \mathcal D_P=1+\sum_{\substack{t=p^n\\p\in P,\ n\ge1}}\frac1{\hgt_P(t)},
 \qquad
 \mathcal R_P=\sum_{u\in\mathcal S_P}\frac1{\Lprefix(u)}.
\]
For $P=\{2,3,5\}$, $\Lprefix(5)=\Lprefix(6)=60$ contributes $1/60$ to
$\mathcal D_P$ and $2/60$ to $\mathcal R_P$. Erd\H{o}s Problem~\#269 asks about
$\mathcal R_P$~\cite[p.~65]{erdosgraham1980} and~\cite[p.~106]{erdos1988}.
Positive powers of distinct primes never coincide; geometric growth of
successive running LCMs gives convergence of $\mathcal D_P$.
We use $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.

\papersectiontarget{r4-five-map-theorem}
\begin{theorem}[the sum over distinct running LCMs for $\{2,3,5\}$]\label{res:distinct-height-235}
The number $\mathcal D_{\{2,3,5\}}$ is irrational.
\end{theorem}

Rationality would leave only finitely many normalised tails, but finiteness
alone does not force the jumps to repeat. The decisive step is to recover
the next block and the following tail from the current tail. Powers of
$2$ delimit the blocks; the spacing of powers of $5$ separates their five
affine images. Equal tails then have identical futures, contradicting
the irrational frequency of powers of $3$.

Erd\H{o}s asserted irrationality of $\mathcal D_P$ for every finite
$P$ with $|P|\ge2$ in a letter dated 1 January 1973, without printing a
proof~\cite[p.~335]{erdos1974letter}. Thus the theorem above is a special
case of that earlier assertion. We claim no priority for its conclusion.
The \longrecord{r3-distinct-proof}{companion's general argument} uses an
isolated interchange of jumps on a torus. That argument is retained there
as an ordinary proof awaiting formalisation. The proof below is independent
of that argument.

Our arguments leave the repeated sum $\mathcal R_P$ unresolved for finite
$P$ with $|P|\ge3$. For $P=\{p\}$ both sums equal $p/(p-1)$.

After the five-map proof in Section~\ref{sec:distinct-235}, we retain the
multiplicities. The bases remain the same, but the block coefficients and
tails grow quadratically. Sections~\ref{sec:lcm} and~\ref{sec:escape} replace
finite-state repetition by a test for excluding integer tails.
For two primes, Fan's factorisation~\cite{fan2026comment} reduces both sums
to a Hecke--Mahler value and yields transcendence
(Section~\ref{sec:two-prime}). The appendices supply the running LCM
identities and show why exact finite separation of the three-prime kernel
cannot extend that factorisation.

\section{Recovering the prime-power jumps}\label{sec:distinct}\label{sec:distinct-235}
Long division combines a finite set of remainders with a deterministic
rule for the next digit and remainder. Here the bases vary with the
prime-power jumps, so that rule must be proved. We first obtain finitely
many tails under rationality, then recover the jumps from each tail.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{res:distinct-height-235}]
\emph{Finitely many tails under rationality.}
Write $\hgt=\hgt_{\{2,3,5\}}$ in this proof and put $P_a=\hgt(2^a)$.
Every running LCM at or before $2^a$ divides $P_a$. We therefore normalise
the tail after $2^a$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:five-tail}
 Y_a=P_a\sum_{\substack{t>2^a\\t=2^n,3^n\text{ or }5^n,\ n\ge1}}
                   \frac1{\hgt(t)}.
\end{equation}
Each subsequent jump multiplies the running LCM by at least $2$, and a jump
by $3$ eventually occurs. Comparison with $\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j}$ gives
$0<Y_a<1$.

Suppose that $\mathcal D_{\{2,3,5\}}=N/K$, where $N$ is an integer and
$K\ge1$ is an integer. Clearing the finite prefix gives
\[
 KY_a=P_aN-K\left(P_a+
        \sum_{\substack{t\le2^a\\t=2^n,3^n\text{ or }5^n,\ n\ge1}}
                 \frac{P_a}{\hgt(t)}\right)\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Thus the $Y_a$ lie in the finite set $(K^{-1}\mathbb Z)\cap(0,1)$.
It remains to show why equality of two tails propagates.

\medskip
\emph{Recovering a block from its tail.}
Consider the jumps between $16$ and $32$, including the last endpoint.
They occur at $25,27,32$, multiplying the running LCM successively by $5,3,2$.
After normalisation at $16$, their contribution is
$1/5+1/15+1/30$. The remaining tail is normalised at a running LCM $30$
times as large, so
\[
 Y_4=\frac15+\frac1{15}+\frac1{30}+\frac{Y_5}{30}
     =\frac{9+Y_5}{30}.
\]
In the block $(64,128]$, the interior jumps occur in the opposite order,
at $81,125$. Its constant term is $1/3+1/15+1/30=13/30$.
The multiplier $30$ records which primes occur, but not their order.
The numerators $9$ and $13$ retain that order. To read it from a tail,
we must also control the unknown following tail.

Every block $(2^a,2^{a+1}]$ contains its terminal power of $2$, at most
one power of $3$ and at most one power of $5$. We record the interior
jumps in their order by a word $\tau_a$ on the letters $3,5$, omitting
the terminal $2$. Splitting off the block gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:five-maps}
 Y_a=G_{\tau_a}(Y_{a+1}),\qquad
 G_\tau(y)=\frac{\mu_\tau+y}{b_\tau},\qquad
 \begin{array}{c|ccccc}
 \tau&\varnothing&3&5&35&53\\\hline
 b_\tau&2&6&10&30&30\\
 \mu_\tau&1&3&3&13&9
 \end{array}
\end{equation}
Here $b_\tau$ is the factor by which the running LCM increases across the
block, and $\mu_\tau/b_\tau$ is the block's normalised contribution.

The bound $0<Y_{a+1}<1$ does not yet recover $\tau_a$:
$G_{53}([0,1])=[3/10,1/3]$ and $G_5([0,1])=[3/10,2/5]$ overlap.
The table improves the lower bound to $Y_a\ge3/10$. To separate these
two images, an upper bound $U$ must satisfy
\[
 G_{53}(U)<G_5(3/10),\qquad
 \frac{9+U}{30}<\frac{33}{100},\qquad U<\frac9{10}.
\]
The spacing of powers of $5$ supplies such a bound.
A power $5^f$ belongs to block $\lfloor f\log_2 5\rfloor$. These
indices start at $2$ and their successive differences are $2$ or $3$.
Every three consecutive blocks therefore contain a power of $5$.
Given $a$, let $j\in\{a,a+1,a+2\}$ be the first such block. The maps
for blocks containing $5$ give $Y_j\le7/15$, since $Y_{j+1}<1$ and
$G_{35}(1)=7/15$ bounds $G_5(1)$ and $G_{53}(1)$ as well.
We now work \emph{backwards} from $j$ to $a$. Each intervening block
has map $G_\varnothing$ or $G_3$, and
$G_3(y)\le G_\varnothing(y)=(1+y)/2$ for $y\ge0$.
At most two backward steps give the successive bounds
$7/15$, $11/15$, $13/15$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:five-interval}
 Y_a\in I=\left[\frac3{10},\frac{13}{15}\right],\qquad
 G_\varnothing\bigl(G_\varnothing(7/15)\bigr)=\frac{13}{15}<\frac9{10}.
\end{equation}
This bound holds for the tails of the prime-power sequence because
every three consecutive blocks contain a power of $5$. The interval
$I$ is not invariant under arbitrary compositions of the five maps:
for example, $G_\varnothing(13/15)=14/15$ lies outside $I$.

Figure~\ref{fig:five-map-images} gives the exact images of $I$. They
are pairwise disjoint, with successive gaps
$1/900,17/300,79/900,1/180$. Writing $L=3/10$ and $U=13/15$, the two
narrow gaps are
\[
 G_5(L)-G_{53}(U)=\frac{3L-U}{30}=\frac1{900},\qquad
 G_\varnothing(L)-G_3(U)=\frac{3L-U}{6}=\frac1{180}.
\]
Thus the same inequality $U<3L=9/10$ separates both pairs.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1cm,y=1cm,font=\small]
  % All five rows use the same horizontal scale, from 3/10 to 19/20.
  \node[anchor=west] at (0,3.65) {$\tau$};
  \node[anchor=west] at (.8,3.65) {$G_\tau(I)$};
  \node[anchor=west] at (4.8,3.65) {Common scale};
  \foreach \y/\name/\lo/\hi in {
    3.05/53/{31/100}/{74/225},
    2.50/5/{33/100}/{29/75},
    1.95/35/{133/300}/{104/225},
    1.40/3/{11/20}/{29/45},
    .85/\varnothing/{13/20}/{14/15}} {
      \node[anchor=west] at (0,\y) {$\name$};
