##### From a Cold Clone to a Proof Receipt

How can a reasoning agent comprehend a large Lean corpus before compiling, then cross into replayable proof authority and incremental validation?

Superseded, and kept here so an existing citation still resolves.

[PDF on GitHub, 12 pages](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/main/paper/systems/cold-clone-to-proof-receipt.pdf) [LaTeX source](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/main/paper/systems/cold-clone-to-proof-receipt.tex) in plectis- erdos

Abstract and reading guide

A large formal library can be mechanically exact and still be practically unreadable to the next reader or reasoning agent. At the audited revision a cold clone exposes a bounded six-line tour over 1,019 Lean modules and 153,238 declarations, a map of ten programmes, 101 curated claims, and an elaborated reference graph, none of which requires a build. 503 of those modules and 8,171 of those declarations are marked machine-generated certificate shards, counted as source and never as claims, and that marking is a classification floor rather than the true generated share, since earlier emitted families predate the markers. Navigation receives no proof authority: probe verdicts come from the pinned Lean process and cannot be authored by the agent, and a claim must cite an accepted probe that replay reruns from stored bytes. The audit was author-operated; no external contributor had completed the tour or documented return path by 31 August 2026.

Explains the agent - navigation architecture: layered corpus projections, bounded intent routing, kernel -authored session receipts, focused builds, and exact dependency - index cache receipts. Not authority for proof validity, optimal reasoning, external mathematical novelty, or demonstrated transfer to another formalisation project.

How can outsiders contribute compute, mathematical direction, architecture, or review without receiving authority to declare a proof?

Abstract and reading guide

A public Lean repository can serve as a shared conversion layer between compute, agent capability, human mathematical direction, infrastructure quality, and review. The paper defines role- bounded work packets, two first-class contribution tracks, provenance and credit, safe untrusted returns, and a candidate-to-attention funnel. Formal verification strengthens one evidence layer; human meaning, novelty, significance, and broad mathematical adoption remain separate. The eight Erdős problems are hard test worlds and all remain open. This is a working prototype; no completed external cold clone or landed outside contribution was recorded by 31 August 2026.

Explains the open- source strategy: how outside compute, mathematics, architecture improvements, review, and credit enter one bounded commons. Not authority for a solution to any Erdős problem, measured discovery-rate improvement, human peer review, novelty, significance, or community endorsement. #### Who built this

My name is Will Cook. My background is economics. I built this research system with AI coding agents and funded the work myself.

AI agents draft and revise the papers from objectives and review criteria I set. I choose what to release and maintain the research record. Each paper identifies the earlier sources and other contributors it draws on.

I am clearly not a mathematician. I try my best to create things that I think of, because it’s fun. I need people who know the field to tell me what’s wrong, or suggest a direction worth pursuing.

For a small example, try [multiplying two polynomial approximations](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/main/docs/reading-edition/enclosure-product-use.md). The question is whether their error bounds guarantee the accuracy of the product. The note credits the original theorem and includes an exact arithmetic checker.

More background: how I got here

It started as a private repo built for a trading system. UK financial regulation meant that seemed too hairy a path to go down without more guidance, but by then I had already built a large financial database, which I probably can’t release. This was before I had even used Claude Code.

I then discovered coding agent apps, and it all changed. I spent months and months building whatever I could come up with. I developed a doctrine for my agents, and built a frontend that would evolve with the backend to be able to see what was happening in the system.

I realised I couldn’t release the entire thing, so I abandoned what I deemed risky and focused on building a new system, Plectis, that would let me showcase cross-sections of the system.

I stopped vibe-mathing and focused on trying to build AI systems, as I realised systems can do a much better job than I could at doing the most abstract repeatable tasks, and in organising work done, and ultimately in directing and planning the efforts of AI at any given moment.

Then I picked eight Erdős problems. I didn’t expect to be able to solve them, the point was the journey getting there and what you can learn from it, so every no-go and failed route gets written down where the next person can use it.

In September a lot of mathematicians wrote about AI and mathematics, and a lot of it lands on the point I started from, that getting a result checked is not the same as understanding it. [De Toffoli and Duede](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/09/12/after-math/) separate a logical proof, which Lean can certify, from an intelligible one that people can understand and build on. [Henry Cohn](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/09/15/the-technical-debt-of-ai-generated-mathematics/) calls unexplained AI proofs technical debt, and asks whoever pushed the button to take responsibility for the result, talk to people in the field and shed light on how it was found. [Bryna Kra](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/09/13/deep-theorems-were-scarce-and-difficult-and-so-became-an-effective-mechanism-to-identify-deep-thought-ai-has-broken-this-system/) wants authors who can explain a proof’s mechanism and how they got there, with discovery, proof, formalisation and explanation credited separately. [Daniel Litt](https://www.daniellitt.com/blog/2026/9/13/a-beginning-for-mathematics/) argues that talks now show understanding better than papers do, and that working out what is interesting is the community’s job. [Grant Sanderson](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/09/18/if-math-is-more-than-proof-we-need-to-better-celebrate-the-rest-of-it/) points out that an AI proof arrives with its explanation still to be written, and no proof assistant will ever check that part. [Terence Tao](https://mathstodon.xyz/@tao/117237320796901560) says the scarce thing now is a promising problem, along with knowing which nearby problems are easy, hard or out of reach. And the [AGMAI recommendations](https://agmai.org/general-sep29/) of 29 September ask AI labs that release mathematics nobody yet understands to cite related work, write it up as a normal paper, formalise it as far as possible, with a Comparator challenge and a formalization.yaml, or state its formalization status if doing that would cause unacceptable delays, and say how AI was used and what it tried and failed.

So that’s basically what I’ve been trying to build as a lay person. Creating a Lean corpus is one thing, but what I think is my main contribution is the pipeline that distils it into papers that try to avoid the common pitfalls of AI-written papers, like just dropping Lean bombs: Lean for the logical part, a short paper for the intelligible part, a long paper for the routes that failed and how hard each nearby question turned out to be, and seminar-style videos we’re trying to automate, because a talk shows whether something is understood. It’s more of a proof of concept than me claiming I understand the mathematics deeply enough to explain it. If someone unknown with no understanding can get even part of the way, it’s an example of what an expert could do with the same tools. I’m not presupposing any of it is good, which is why the claims link to their evidence and why I need people who know the field to tell me what’s wrong.

Human mathematicians are meant to provide the direction. I’ve been struggling to get it, so a lot of this is me seeing how far you can get without it. Ideally a mathematician glances through, finds an idea worth their time, and either works on it themselves or emails me a direction, and we take that as the seed and get agents to attack it, given all of the failed routes and the short paper as it stands. When someone has told me what was wrong, it changed the work, and the [credit ledger](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/main/docs/research-commons/CREDIT_LEDGER.md) lists every case, with names withheld until each person says they’re happy to be named.

My biggest problem has been that nobody with expertise can really judge the entire thing, because it spans so many domains.

You will get the credit. I just want my system used.

Thank you for your time and interest.

#### What OpenAI published

OpenAI labels [189](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/numbers.html#n-statements_lean_main_results) of the [416](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/numbers.html#n-statements_lean) Lean statement files as main results in its Lean catalogue.

The papers cite one another in [586](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/numbers.html#n-internal_citation_edges) directed pairs and cite [11,019](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/numbers.html#n-external_works_cited) works outside the release. OpenAI has withdrawn [3](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/numbers.html#n-manuscripts_withdrawn) papers and replaced [27](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/numbers.html#n-manuscripts_previous_editions) with later editions.

Atlas links public contributions credited to [371](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/numbers.html#n-community_people) names and places [671](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/numbers.html#n-community_findings) reports beside the results they discuss.

[See what each number counts](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/numbers.html)

#### Who examined the release, and how

These groups report different kinds of work: verifying a formal proof with a program, comparing a Lean statement with a paper, or testing a finite claim by calculation. Atlas links their original reports and has not repeated their work.
- [Carlos Toledo, cert-machine](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/sources.html#src-cert-machine) ran Comparator on OpenAI’s proofs with a second independent verifier, tested finite claims in some papers by exact calculation, and compared the Lean statements with OpenAI’s catalogue descriptions.
- [MathVet](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/sources.html#src-mathvet) ran Comparator on OpenAI’s proofs in an isolated environment and compared the Lean statements with OpenAI’s catalogue descriptions under published assessment rules.
- [Neal McBurnett, openai-math-lean-tooling](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/sources.html#src-nealmcb-lean-tooling) ran Comparator on OpenAI’s proofs using Lean’s own proof verifier and recorded the time and memory used.
- [Ben Knill, openai-math-hol-cards](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/sources.html#src-hol-cards) proved selected intermediate steps using HOL Light, a different proof assistant, and tested incorrect examples that the program should reject.
- [Thomas Bloom, erdosproblems.com](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/sources.html#src-erdos-problems) identifies which Erdős problems the papers address. These links do not assess whether the claimed proofs are correct.

[Every source, with what each one reports](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/sources.html)

#### How to help

Each contribution covers one result or one page, and is credited by name on the pages it changes.

##### Without an AI account

Open a short GitHub form to explain a result, compare a Lean statement with its paper, or report a problem with a page.

[Ways to contribute](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/contribute.html)

##### With an AI account

Give your assistant the start-here guide from the repository. It helps you choose one useful note, drafts it privately and leaves the signing to you.

[The start-here guide](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-atlas/tree/main/skills/start-here)

Some Lean statements have a specific reason to be read first. [See which, and why](https://wcook04.github.io/plectis-atlas/explain.html#careful-reading)

# Zenith: programs, experiments and useful memory

> Public research into executable programs, measured investigations and useful memory. Experiments retain explicit limitations and source provenance.

## Start here

- [Agent map](agent-map.md): chapters, source documents, evidence and navigable dependency graphs; no JavaScript required.
- [Machine route index](agent-index.json): maps every public API request, including mission/profile queries, to a directly fetchable JSON file.
- [Reading website](./): human reading experience.
- [Export provenance](snapshot-manifest.json): hashes for the published machine-readable files.

## Research sources

- [introduction](api/v1/documents/introduction.json): source text and provenance.
- [results](api/v1/documents/results.json): source text and provenance.
- [research-programme](api/v1/documents/research-programme.json): source text and provenance.
- [notice](api/v1/documents/notice.json): source text and provenance.

Read the source-bound evidence before making a result claim. Graph edges are authored prerequisites, not measured execution. Keep historical profiles separate. This index is a discovery aid; it does not change crawler access policy.
